Acanthite

Acanthite is the monoclinic silver sulfide mineral Ag2S, listed as grandfathered with original-description year 1855 in the September 2026 IMA master list. It is distinct from elemental silver, generic silver-containing nanoparticles and the high-temperature cubic Ag2S form commonly called argentite. A laboratory bacterial study identifies acanthite as a minority particle type within a mixed silver-containing population. No criticality designation is inherited from silver.

Acid mine drainage

Acidic, metal- and sulfate-bearing drainage generated when mining exposes sulfide-bearing materials to oxidation. This record denotes the heterogeneous liquid mine-derived feed, distinct from natural ore, individual dissolved elements, coal-mine-drainage treatment solids, and isolated precipitate phases. The characterized Brazilian copper-mine and South African mining-facility waters below are separate source-specific samples, not a universal composition or interchangeable reactor feed. No constituent criticality designation or industrial recovery performance is transferred to this resource.

Adamsite-(Y)

Hydrated sodium-yttrium carbonate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula NaY(CO3)2(H2O)3·3H2O and approval number IMA 1999-020. Grice, Gault, Roberts, and Cooper (2000) described the cotype specimens (CMNMC 82939 and CMNMC 82940, formerly provisional phases UK 96 and UK 106) from the Poudrette dike, Poudrette quarry, Mont Saint-Hilaire, Rouville County, Quebec, Canada, where it occurs with Petersenite-(Ce), shomiokite-(Y), thomasclarkite-(Y), donnayite-(Y), and rhodochrosite. Electron-microprobe WDS analysis (7 analyses on 3 crystals, p. 1460) combined with thermogravimetric analysis yielded Na2O 8.64, CaO 0.05, Y2O3 22.88, Ce2O3 0.37, Nd2O3 1.41, Sm2O3 1.02, Gd2O3 1.92, Tb2O3 0.56, Dy2O3 3.28, Ho2O3 0.90, Er2O3 2.83, Tm2O3 0.27, Yb2O3 1.04, CO2 25.10 (12.9 wt% evolved in TGA plus 12.2 wt% ideal non-evolved), H2O 29.90, total 100.17 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 12 O atoms to the empirical formula Na1.00(Y0.72Dy0.06Er0.05Gd0.04Nd0.03Yb0.02Sm0.02Ho0.02Ce0.01Tb0.01Tm0.01)Sigma0.99C2.04H11.87O12. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction refined in triclinic space group P-1 (a = 6.2592(4), b = 13.0838(7), c = 13.2271(5) A, alpha = 91.130(1), beta = 103.554(1), gamma = 90.188(1) degrees, V = 1052.8(1) A3, Z = 4, R = 0.046, wR = 0.058 for 3338 observed reflections with |Fo| > 5sigma(Fo); powder XRD cell a = 6.262(2), b = 13.047(6), c = 13.220(5) A, alpha = 91.17(4), beta = 103.70(4), gamma = 89.99(4) degrees, V = 1049.1(5) A3) established a layered [Y(CO3)2(H2O)]- sheet structure alternating with [Na(H2O)5]+ polyhedra and unbonded interstitial H2O molecules; hydrogen positions were inferred from O...O distances rather than refined directly. Thermogravimetric analysis under dry nitrogen demonstrated two major multi-step weight-loss intervals up to 590 degrees C, and the mineral readily dissolves with strong effervescence in 10% HCl and decrepitates in acetone or alcohol. Distinct from shomiokite-(Y), thomasclarkite-(Y), piilonenite-(Nd), and elemental yttrium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery process is asserted.

Akaganeite

Akaganeite is a distinct iron oxyhydroxide mineral species, listed with formula (Fe(III),Ni(II))8(OH,O)16Cl1.25·nH2O, renamed status (Rn), and IMA number 1962-004 in the September 2026 IMA master list. The experimental abbreviation beta-FeOOH identifies the synthetic phase assignment used by the study; it does not establish the ideal IMA composition or nickel content of that preparation. This record is separate from iron element, other iron oxyhydroxide species, iron-ore commodities, and mixed waste feeds. No constituent criticality designation is inherited.

Alabandite

Alabandite is the cubic manganese sulfide mineral, ideal formula MnS, grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA list. It is distinct from the MnS polymorph rambergite, elemental manganese and a whole polymetallic ore. The accepted experiment identifies alabandite as one component of natural Talvivaara black shale and measures its content in fractions from laboratory flotation with freeze-dried bacterial biomass. This is not pure-mineral testing, proof of a microbial surface mechanism, manganese product recovery or a criticality designation inherited from Mn.

Albite

Albite is the triclinic sodium feldspar mineral with ideal formula NaAlSi3O8. The September 2026 IMA list marks it grandfathered (G; historical year 1815), not with a numbered approval accession. It is distinct from the feldspar commodity, the potassium-feldspar family, other plagioclase compositions and mixed ores containing albite. The accepted dissolution evidence concerns source-identified Amelia clevelandite under abiotic laboratory conditions; neither microbial activity nor criticality is inferred from elemental composition.

Alburnite

Alburnite is the natural silver-germanium sulfide-telluride mineral Ag8GeTe2S4, listed as approved IMA 2012-073 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The original 2013 approval announcement identifies the Cârnicel vein, Roşia Montană deposit, Apuseni Mountains, Romania, as its type locality. This species remains distinct from argyrodite and from generic Te-bearing material historically called argyrodite. A 2016 study of a Măgura vein specimen reported an arsenic-bearing phase as alburnite using optical microscopy and SEM-EDS, but explicitly left its identity unresolved: it could have alburnite symmetry or be a distinct phase. Its nonstoichiometric, silver-excess EDS result is not treated here as a confirmed alburnite composition. That paper also corrects the authors' 2015 report of associated Cu-Fe-bearing sulfotellurides, attributing the earlier signals to a SEM charge- compensation artifact involving neighboring chalcopyrite; this is not a correction of the 2014 alburnite description. The complete 2014 description and its graphics were not available for this curation, so their quantitative and structural detail remains deferred. No extraction mechanism, recovery performance or constituent-element criticality designation is assigned to this mineral.

Alicewilsonite-(YCe)

A sodium-strontium-yttrium-cerium carbonate mineral approved as IMA 2020-055, with ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula Na2Sr2YCe(CO3)6(H2O)3. The YCe suffix reflects dominance at different crystallographic sites, not a ranking of bulk rare-earth concentrations. This species is distinct from donnayite-(Y), alicewilsonite-(YLa), individual elements and mixed ores. Lykova et al. (2023, Part 2) characterized holotype CMNMC 53660 from Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada, previously labelled donnayite-(Y). The zoned crystal contains an outer alicewilsonite-(YCe) rim and an inner donnayite-(Y)/gaidonnayite assemblage; the single-crystal diffraction grain was selected from the alicewilsonite rim. Wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe measurements used 20 kV, 10 nA, grain-dependent 20–50 micrometre beams and corrections for beam instability. Table 1 reports holotype means of 8.52 wt% Y2O3 and 9.52 wt% Ce2O3 from six analyses. CO2 and H2O were calculated because insufficient pure material could be isolated; infrared spectra support water qualitatively. The 293 K single-crystal refinement gives triclinic P1 and R1 = 0.055 with an 87:13 twin model. Crystal quality limits structural detail: hydrogen was not reliably located, Ca was omitted from the model, and Ce and Dy represented lighter and heavier lanthanides as scattering proxies. Main-text Sr1 site composition uses Ce0.23 whereas Table 4 and the official CIF use Ce0.22; Table 3's Rint of 0.062 also differs from the CIF agreement field of 0.0394. These unresolved differences prevent unqualified reuse of detailed model occupancies or agreement statistics. Natural intergrowths and proposed replacement relations are geological interpretations, not controlled conversion experiments. Qualitative room-temperature dissolution with effervescence in aqueous HCl lacks specified concentration, time and yield, and is not curated as an extraction or recovery mechanism. No microbial process, industrial deployment or transferred elemental criticality is established by this characterization.

Alicewilsonite-(YLa)

An approved sodium-strontium-yttrium-lanthanum carbonate mineral, IMA 2021-047, with ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula Na2Sr2YLa(CO3)6(H2O)3. Its suffix denotes dominance at different crystallographic sites, not a bulk elemental ranking. Lykova et al. (2024, Part 4) characterized holotype CMNMC 89063 from the Paratoo copper mine, South Australia; the structure-determination portion is KNR 44330 in Oslo. Table 1 averages seven electron-microprobe analyses: 9.59 wt% Y2O3 and 11.74 wt% La2O3. Measurements used 20 kV, 10 nA and a 30 micrometre beam with beam-instability corrections. Ce was below detection, not demonstrated absent. CO2 and H2O were calculated because material was scarce; infrared data support water qualitatively. The 293 K single-crystal model is triclinic P1, R1 = 0.058, with a 22:78 twin model. La and Dy served as lanthanide scattering proxies; assigned cation occupancies and half-occupied split carbonate/water sites depend on constraints. Poor crystal quality limits localization and hydrogen was not located. Water-site labels in Table 4 and the official CIF differ, so detailed label-specific bonding is not asserted. This species differs from alicewilsonite-(YCe), donnayite-(Y), elements and mixed mine resources. Its natural secondary geological occurrence does not make it a secondary resource. The discussion's inferred Ce fractionation is not a controlled experiment on this mineral; qualitative room-temperature HCl effervescence lacks specified acid concentration, duration and yield. No extraction mechanism, microbial process, industrial deployment or transferred elemental criticality is established here.

Allanite concentrate

A geological rare-earth-bearing feed represented by the REE-concentrated crushed allanite ore supplied as Zappall from WRE in Schmitz et al. (2025). The paper also calls this material allanite mineral sand. Its generic allanite designation does not establish a particular allanite species, phase purity, mine of origin or commercial grade. This concentrated primary resource is distinct from an ideal mineral species, elemental rare earths, their commodities and secondary waste. No constituent criticality designation is inherited.

Allanite-derived rare-earth leachate

A rare-earth-bearing processing liquor generated from allanite ore, represented here by the chemically purified and reconstituted Halleck Creek, Wyoming feed used by Lu et al. (2026). Acid leaching, impurity precipitation, REE hydroxide precipitation and hydrochloric-acid redissolution precede the biological-reagent experiment. This processing intermediate is distinct from geological ore, beneficiated allanite concentrate, a pure allanite species and an isolated REE product. Its classification reflects chemical processing, not extraction alone. No criticality designation is inherited from its constituents.

Alumina

Aluminium oxide considered as a refined commercial material, used as feed for aluminium smelting and in nonmetallurgical applications such as ceramics, abrasives and refractories. This commodity is distinct from aluminium metal, aluminium hydroxide, bauxite ore and red mud. The broad commodity does not establish a particular crystalline phase or high-purity product specification. The EU designations explicitly name alumina as the intermediate processing form within the combined bauxite/alumina/aluminium value chain. No microbial mechanism is asserted here.

Aluminium salt slag

Salt-flux-bearing mixed slag from aluminium scrap remelting, containing process salts and oxide-rich solids. The accepted study sampled a rotary furnace batch from a Brazilian recycler using NaCl/KCl flux. This resource is defined by salt-flux remelting origin, distinct from the existing post-metal-recovery secondary aluminium dross specimen, generic smelting slag, bauxite residue, elemental aluminium or a single mineral. Laboratory water leaching and recovered salt crystals are documented; microbial action, inherited criticality and industrial deployment of this recipe are not.

Alunite

Alunite is the potassium aluminium hydroxysulfate mineral KAl3(SO4)2(OH)6, listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as redefined, 1987 s.p. It is a distinct species within the alunite group, not a label for every aluminium sulfate or mixed mining residue. Zhong et al. (2019) examined a natural alunite-bearing ore containing quartz and kaolinite. Their laboratory CaO-assisted thermal treatment followed by water leaching increased soluble potassium under selected conditions; the separate evaporation product remained a mixture of potassium/calcium sulfate phases. The accepted experiment is abiotic and does not establish microbial extraction, a pure potassium product, complete aluminium recovery, or industrial deployment. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Amblygonite

Amblygonite is the fluorine-dominant lithium aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula LiAl(PO4)F, distinct from hydroxyl-dominant montebrasite and from lithium as an element. Natural crystals form a substituted F/OH series rather than necessarily pure endmembers. Groat2003 provides primary neutron-diffraction and NMR evidence for this series, including F-rich natural specimens. Triclinic P-1 and the centered C-1 convention describe settings of the same structure. A separate thesis reports heating of a natural specimen labelled amblygonite, but its mixed starting material and conflicting fluorine estimates straddle the species boundary. The thermal observation is retained only for that author-assigned specimen, not as a universal amblygonite decomposition threshold, microbial mechanism or lithium recovery yield.

Ameghinite

Ameghinite is the approved sodium-borate mineral NaB3O3(OH)4, IMA1966-034, in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The original Tincalayu, Salta, Argentina specimens contained ameghinite nodules separated from surrounding borax by tincalconite. The 1967 chemical aliquot retained an optically estimated two percent tincalconite; its analysis is not a pure end-member composition. Dal Negro, Martin Pozas and Ungaretti's 1975 single-crystal study established a C2/c structure with isolated triborate units, each containing one boron tetrahedron and two triangles, linked through sodium coordination and hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen positions were found in difference-Fourier maps; the study did not supply a new bulk chemical assay of its fragment. The distinct sodium hexaborate tetrahydrate produced in Xiong et al.'s 2017 borax experiments was described as an ameghinite polymorph and possible precursor, not as experimentally demonstrated formation of ameghinite. This mineral species is distinct from elemental boron and the borates commodity; criticality and microbial activity are not inferred.

IMA:1966-034
Ammonioborite

Grandfathered hydrated ammonium pentaborate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (NH4)3B15O20(OH)8(H2O)4, status G, and original-description year 1933 (not a numbered IMA approval CURIE). Schaller (1933) described ammonioborite from the boric-acid fumaroles (soffioni) of Larderello, Tuscany, Italy, on specimens in the US National Museum (including USNM 93756, 94172, and Roebling R6167) intergrown with sassolite (boric acid, B(OH)3). Utilizing the faster dissolution of sassolite in cold water (0.2 g artificial sassolite dissolved in 75 mL cold water within 15 min, whereas ammonioborite required more than 2 h), Schaller isolated 93 mg of purified ammonioborite for wet-chemical titration (Table 5, p. 488: (NH4)2O 9.78 wt%, B2O3 74.18 wt%, H2O by difference 16.04 wt%), proposing the oxide ratio (NH4)2O·5B2O3·5H2O (equivalent to (NH4)2B10O16·5H2O) and distinguishing it from larderellite by optical refractive indices (alpha = 1.470, beta = 1.487, gamma = 1.540) and Posnjak's X-ray powder photographs (Figure 2, p. 490). Schaller reported that laboratory crystallization trials from aqueous boric- acid and ammonia solutions at room temperature yielded only the orthorhombic synthetic 1:5:8 hydrate (NH4)2O·5B2O3·8H2O and failed to synthesize ammonioborite. The later crystal-structure determination by Merlino and Sartori (Science 171 (1971), 377), which established the current polyborate formula (NH4)3B15O20(OH)8(H2O)4 (oxide ratio 3(NH4)2O·15B2O3·16H2O, i.e. 1:5:5.33), is cited in the IMA Master List but is behind a paywall and was not independently acquired at curation. Distinct from larderellite, sassolite, elemental boron, and borate commodities; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Ammoniojarosite

Ammoniojarosite is the ammonium ferric hydroxysulfate mineral with ideal formula (NH4)Fe3(SO4)2(OH)6, with ferric iron. The September 2026 IMA list records it as redefined, 1987 s.p. It is distinct from potassium jarosite, natrojarosite, hydroniumjarosite and industrial jarosite residues. Wang et al. (2007) prepared diffraction-assigned ammoniojarosite during biological oxidation of ferrous sulfate in ammonium-containing laboratory media. Their products were nonstoichiometric, and low-ammonium experiments instead produced schwertmannite or mixed precipitates. Neither phase assignment nor bulk composition establishes absolute phase purity, a recovered-metal yield, microbial necessity or industrial deployment. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Anatase

Anatase is the TiO2 mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with approved status A and the designation 1962 s.p. The latter denotes a special procedure, not a numbered approval identifier. Anatase is distinct from rutile and brookite despite their common ideal formula, and from elemental titanium, titanium-bearing ores and unspecified TiO2 nanoparticles. The curated experiment concerns a manufactured anatase counterpart produced using engineered bacterial biomass, a soluble titanium reagent and subsequent heat treatment. It does not establish microbial formation of natural anatase, dissolution of a natural titanium mineral or recovery of titanium from an ore or waste. No constituent-derived criticality is asserted.

Ancylite-(Ce)

A natural cerium-strontium carbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula CeSr(CO3)2(OH)(H2O). The authority lists renamed status and 1987 special procedure, not a numbered approval accession. The 2024 approved ancylite-supergroup nomenclature distinguishes this Sr-dominant, Ce-dominant species from Ca-dominant calcioancylites and from kozoites. In its general formula, x is the trivalent-cation content per two cations; the ancylite group spans 1 <= x <= 1.5, whereas the kozoite group spans 1.5 < x <= 2. Dal Negro et al. (1975) studied a natural crystal from a nepheline-syenite pegmatite at Mont Saint-Hilaire, Quebec. Their Table 2 composition, La0.56Ce0.82Sr0.40Ca0.22(CO3)2(OH)1.38 ·0.62H2O, is a mixed-REE specimen formula, distinct from the ideal endmember. Five-grain microprobe averages were normalized using a separate thermogravimetric loss; water and carbon dioxide could not be individually determined from that curve. The text's assumed 20:80 water-to-carbon-dioxide loss partition does not match the individual volatile values in Table 1. Those values are not independent measured water and carbon dioxide contents. A crystal fragment was refined in orthorhombic Pmcn, a nonstandard setting of Pnma, to R = 0.059 using 498 observed reflections. The model places mixed heavy cations on a shared site, with eight carbonate oxygen neighbours and two hydroxyl or water oxygen neighbours; it does not locate hydrogen atoms or independently resolve the separate cation occupancies. Tables 3–6 include coordinates, displacement parameters, distances and structure factors. Structural comparisons with aragonite and bastnaesite are interpretations, not observed mineral conversions. No mineral-specific extraction experiment, microbial mechanism, recovery yield, industrial deployment or inherited criticality designation is asserted.

Andersonite

Andersonite is the sodium calcium uranyl carbonate hydrate mineral with the September 2026 IMA formula Na2Ca(UO2)(CO3)3(H2O)6. Its grandfathered status G and original-description year 1951 are not an approval accession. A natural Cane Springs Canyon specimen studied in 2018 was refined in trigonal R-3m with 5.3 H2O per formula unit, distinct from the ideal six-water formula and from synthetic preparations. The authors proposed variable channel-water occupancy and a (5+x)H2O formulation; that proposal does not replace the current IMA formula here. This mineral is distinct from elemental uranium and a uranium commodity. No criticality designation, microbial process or industrial recovery is inferred.

Argentojarosite

Argentojarosite is the silver ferric hydroxysulfate mineral with ideal formula AgFe3(SO4)2(OH)6, with ferric iron. The September 2026 IMA list records it as redefined, 1987 s.p. It is distinct from potassium jarosite and from silver ions, metallic silver or a generic industrial jarosite precipitate. Mukherjee's 2013 Ohio State MSc thesis identified synthetic argentojarosite following silver-nitrate addition to an iron-oxidizing culture's ferric sulfate and poorly crystalline ferric precipitates. Argyrodite

Argyrodite is the silver-germanium sulfide mineral species Ag8GeS6, listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as grandfathered, with 1886 as the original-description year rather than an IMA approval number. Ono and Sato's 1995 study identified natural argyrodite in fine-grained massive black ore from the Ezuri Kuroko deposit, Japan, using reflected-light microscopy and electron-microprobe analysis. Figure 3F shows the mineral with galena, covellite, chalcopyrite and bornite in barite; Table 2 gives a specimen analysis described as close to ideal Ag8GeS6, with minor Cu, Fe and As. This specimen observation does not establish uniform composition, bulk germanium grade, resource size or recovery yield. The authors' fluid-inclusion measurements concern sphalerite and their formation-temperature interpretation is not an argyrodite extraction assay. This natural species is distinct from synthetic lithium argyrodite electrolytes and from the separately recognized alburnite, Ag8GeTe2S4. Historical Te-rich argyrodite reports from Roşia Montană are not used here as interchangeable composition evidence: the 2014 alburnite description explicitly revisits the earlier interpretation. Handbook crystallographic citations to synthetic Ag8GeS6 are not treated as measurements of the Ezuri specimen. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery performance or inherited constituent-element criticality designation is assigned.

Aristarainite

Aristarainite is the approved sodium-magnesium borate mineral Na2Mg[B6O8(OH)4]2·4H2O, IMA1973-029, in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Hurlbut and Erd described natural crystals from the Tincalayu borax deposit, Salta, Argentina, including material separated from borax/kernite hosts with warm water. Their 1974 chemical analysis on 95.4 mg included potassium and yielded the historical oxide formula Na2O·MgO·6B2O3·10H2O. Ghose and Wan's 1977 single-crystal refinement revised that ideal hydration to eight oxide-formula waters, equivalent to the current structural formula. This revision came from the structural model, not a new bulk-water assay. Hexaborate units form chains parallel to b; magnesium and sodium link these into sheets parallel to (001), cross-linked by hydrogen bonds. One hydrogen on the O(14) water site was modeled as two half-occupied positions; this is crystallographic disorder, not a measured molecular-motion rate. The papers' qualitative water/acid solubility and proposed geological polymerization do not establish extraction kinetics or an engineered process. Species identity is distinct from the borates commodity and its constituent elements; no criticality, microbial mechanism or industrial recovery claim is inferred.

Autunite

Autunite is a calcium uranyl phosphate mineral with formula Ca(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)11 in the September 2026 IMA list, which assigns grandfathered status G and original-description year 1852; that year is not a numbered IMA approval. Locock and Burns characterized a synthetic crystal grown over four months by diffusion of phosphate and uranyl nitrate into calcium-bearing silica gel, not a natural specimen. They sealed the crystal with diluted growth solution to limit rapid air dehydration and refined an orthorhombic Pnma structure containing sheets of uranyl square bipyramids linked to phosphate tetrahedra. Calcium has seven coordinating water groups and two longer contacts to uranyl apical oxygen atoms. The refined Ca-site occupancy was 86.0(7)%, so this experimental crystal is not established as a fully occupied ideal endmember; charge compensation by oxonium was proposed rather than directly demonstrated. Hydrogen positions were derived from difference maps and crystal-chemical arguments with bond-length constraints and fixed displacement parameters; the proposed hydrogen-bond network is not an unconstrained determination of every hydrogen position. The dependent publisher deposits contain anisotropic parameters and 4318 unique indexed reflections, matching the reported unique-reflection count, but their inspection is not an independent refinement or replication. The paper proposes loss of two independent interstitial-water sites to yield a seven-water calcium phase; this structural proposal does not establish the product as the six-water meta-autunite species in the current IMA list. Autunite is distinct from meta-autunite, the autunite mineral group, uranyl ions and elemental uranium. No microbial extraction, isolated-product recovery, industrial deployment or inherited uranium criticality is asserted by this identity record.

Baddeleyite

Baddeleyite is the natural monoclinic zirconium oxide mineral species ZrO2, listed as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. It is distinct from elemental zirconium, zircon (ZrSiO4), synthetic zirconia products and other ZrO2 polymorphs. Huraiová, Hurai and Konečný (2011) characterized baddeleyite associated with a zoned zircon crystal separated from redeposited sediments of the Hajnáčka-Kostná dolina basaltic maar, southern Slovakia. Cathodoluminescence and backscattered-electron images show baddeleyite in melt pockets and in a reaction rim intergrown with sanidine and anorthoclase. Their Table 2 reports six representative baddeleyite microprobe analyses containing 96.65-98.27 wt.% ZrO2 and 0.99-1.06 wt.% HfO2, alongside analyses of the distinct host zircon. These oxide-equivalent specimen compositions are not elemental-metal percentages, mineral-wide purity or resource grades. The study uses microscopy and electron microprobe chemistry; it does not report a new diffraction refinement. Formation by reaction of zircon with Si-poor, Al-rich melt is the authors' geological interpretation, not a controlled transformation experiment. The reported absence of light rare earth elements is bounded by analytical detection limits, not proof of zero concentration. This identity and natural-occurrence evidence does not establish microbial extraction, recovery, industrial deployment or a dated criticality designation for the mineral.

Bainbridgeite-(NdCe)

Anhydrous-layer-free hydrated sodium-barium-rare-earth carbonate mineral of the mckelveyite group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula Na2Ba2NdCe(CO3)6(H2O)3 and approval number IMA 2023-018. Lykova et al. (2026) characterized the holotype specimen (CMNMC 90534, where bainbridgeite-(NdCe) forms 20-30 um outer rims on barrel-shaped crystals over a bainbridgeite-(YCe) core CMNMC 46324 and an intermediate bainbridgeite-(YCe)-alicewilsonite-(YCe) zone in a carbonate pegmatite) and a second hornfels occurrence (CMNMC 52468, tabular crystals up to 0.5 mm) from the Poudrette (Demix) quarry, Mont Saint-Hilaire, Rouville County, Quebec, Canada. Wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analysis on holotype CMNMC 90534 (7 analyses, Table 1, p. 422) yielded Na2O 6.85, CaO 1.16, SrO 4.83, BaO 24.02, Y2O3 1.84, La2O3 6.07, Ce2O3 8.82, Pr2O3 0.76, Nd2O3 6.24, Sm2O3 3.34, Eu2O3 0.46, Gd2O3 2.74, Tb2O3 0.21, Dy2O3 0.53, ThO2 0.24, CO2* 27.33, H2O* 5.73, total 101.17 wt%, corresponding to the empirical formula Na2.09Ca0.19Sr0.44Ba1.48Y0.15La0.35Ce0.51Pr0.04Nd0.35Sm0.18Eu0.03Gd0.14Tb0.01Dy0.03Th0.01(CO3)5.86(H2O)3.00 (with CO2 and H2O calculated from stoichiometry and structure rather than directly assayed). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 293 K refined in triclinic space group P1 (a = 9.0525(3), b = 9.1178(2), c = 6.85180(19) A, alpha = 102.575(3), beta = 116.272(4), gamma = 59.788(4) degrees, V = 438.23(3) A3, Z = 1, R1 = 0.036, wR2 = 0.099 for 4140 independent reflections with I > 2sigma(I)) established a weloganite-type structure with six independent large cation sites (Ba1, Ba2, Ce3, Na4, Na5, Nd6), where light lanthanoids (Ce, La, Pr) partition into the larger 10-coordinated Ce3 polyhedron (Ce0.75Ba0.15Sr0.10) while Nd, heavier lanthanoids (Sm, Gd), and Y partition into the smaller 9-coordinated Nd6 polyhedron (Nd0.37Y0.33Na0.17Gd0.13; the refined Y occupancy exceeds the 0.15 apfu WDS rim average because the diffraction crystal included both the bainbridgeite-(NdCe) rim and bainbridgeite-(YCe) core). This intra-crystalline lanthanoid partitioning is a natural crystal-chemical observation, not a laboratory separation process. Distinct from bainbridgeite-(YCe), alicewilsonite-(YCe), mckelveyite-(Y), and elemental neodymium or cerium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or recovery yield is asserted.

IMA:2023-018
Bainbridgeite-(YCe)

An approved sodium-barium-yttrium-cerium carbonate mineral, IMA 2020-065, with ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula Na2Ba2YCe(CO3)6(H2O)3. The suffix denotes dominant cations at distinct crystallographic sites. Lykova et al. (2024, Part 3) characterized holotype CMNMC 46324 from Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada. Its five electron-microprobe analyses average 8.24 wt% Y2O3 and 8.38 wt% Ce2O3 (Table 1); the other specimens in that table are separate. Analyses used 20 kV, 10 nA, 20–50 micrometre beams and beam-instability corrections. CO2 and H2O were calculated, not measured; infrared data support water qualitatively. The 293 K single-crystal model is triclinic P1, R1 = 0.040, with twinning. Poor crystal quality, omitted Ca, Ce/Dy scattering proxies for lighter/heavier lanthanides, constrained occupancies and unlocated hydrogen limit atom-specific interpretation. Table 6 gives unequal measured and assigned-model scattering values for Y6 (40.1 versus 38.3 electrons). The 2026 Part 5 follow-up identifies a bainbridgeite-(NdCe) rim on the photographed YCe holotype crystal, with a YCe core and an intermediate YCe/alicewilsonite-(YCe) zone. Accordingly, the 2024 chemistry is a specimen-resolved analysis, not a homogeneous whole-crystal assay; the 2026 mixed-phase diffraction model is not substituted for it. This mineral is distinct from bainbridgeite-(NdCe), alicewilsonite-(YCe), elements and ores. Natural intergrowth and proposed geological replacement are not controlled transformation evidence. The qualitative aqueous-HCl effervescence observation has no concentration, duration or yield and is not curated as recovery. No microbial process, industrial deployment or inherited elemental criticality is established by these characterizations.

CHEBI:30501
Beudantite

Beudantite is the lead ferric arsenate-sulfate hydroxide mineral with ideal formula PbFe3(AsO4)(SO4)(OH)6, distinct from phosphate-bearing corkite, plumbojarosite, segnitite and elemental lead or arsenic. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987; that date is not an individual approval accession. Szymański (1988) examined compositionally zoned natural material from Tsumeb, Namibia. Electron-microprobe analyses showed variable Al substitution for Fe and variable As/S ratios rather than a uniform ideal endmember. The accepted single-crystal refinement was crystal 2, with a = 7.3151(9) and c = 17.0355(5) angstrom, R-3m symmetry, 644 unique reflections and a final R factor of 3.7 percent. It supported disordered As/S sites and displaced Pb positions. Crystal 1 had unresolved diffraction-profile problems; crystal 3 showed a slight triclinic distortion but could not be satisfactorily refined and its composition was not determined. Neither the preferred symmetry nor the proposed Pb lone-pair explanation is generalized to every specimen. The article's separately deposited structure-factor Table 4 was not acquired; the published experimental methods, Tables 1-3/5 and Figures 1-3 support this bounded identity assessment. Bari et al. (2024) provide adjacent abiotic dissolution context for a synthetic solid they call beudantite. Its reported bulk formula, Pb0.32(H3O)0.68Fe3(AsO4)0.32(SO4)1.68(OH)6, differs markedly from the ideal species, and initial TEM-EDX detected grains lacking both As and Pb. Their 56-day tests at initial pH 2, 4, 6 and 8 used 0.06 g solid in 40 mL solution at 22 degrees C with triplicate sacrificial sampling. Filtered aqueous element contents, residual diffraction and arsenic X-ray absorption measurements describe that substituted, heterogeneous preparation. Greater mobilization at pH 2 and persistent residual diffraction do not establish dissolution rates or long-term stability of pure natural beudantite. No phase-specific dissolution mechanism is assigned here from those data. The source's inconsistent Fe unit, duplicated sulfate in its reaction equation, and comparison to an ideal Fe/Pb ratio despite the measured composition are not adopted as quantitative or balanced-reaction claims. These sources do not establish microbial transformation, isolated-product recovery or industrial operation. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Billietite

Billietite is the barium uranyl oxide hydroxide hydrate mineral Ba(UO2)6O4(OH)6(H2O)8, distinct from elemental uranium, barium commodities and other uranyl oxide hydrates. The September 2026 IMA list gives grandfathered status G; 1947 is its original-description year, not an approval accession. Finch and colleagues refined a natural Shaba, Democratic Republic of Congo crystal in orthorhombic Pbn21, with two distinct uranyl polyhedral sheets linked by barium and interlayer water. Their eight-water refinement supersedes the incomplete four-water structural model discussed in that paper. Hydrogen bonding was inferred from geometry and bond valence; it was not a direct localization of all hydrogen atoms. The natural crystal used for structure refinement and the specimens used for surface experiments are separate evidence populations. No criticality, microbial mechanism or industrial recovery is inferred.

Briartite is the copper-iron-germanium sulfide mineral species Cu2FeGeS4, listed as approved, IMA 1965-018, by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026. Francotte and colleagues' 1965 description used the broader historical formula Cu2(Fe,Zn)GeS4 and combined polished-section observations, powder X-ray diffraction and electron-microprobe analyses of natural material from Kipushi, with comparative Tsumeb chemistry. Its Fe-Zn variation and uncertain structural interpretation do not establish that every historical analysis belongs to the currently delimited Fe species. The dated IMA list separately recognizes zincobriartite, Cu2ZnGeS4, IMA 2015-094; zinc-rich historical material is not silently reassigned to this briartite record. The original describes small grains and intergrowths with other sulfides, including chalcopyrite, renierite and sphalerite, rather than a pure bulk ore feed. Its Table III column labels conflict with the accompanying prose, so individual assay rows are not imported as unambiguous specimen measurements. Briartite is distinct from germanium element, germanite, renierite and a mixed copper-zinc ore. These mineralogical observations establish neither a microbial recovery mechanism nor industrial extraction performance; no constituent-element criticality designation is inherited.

Brookite

Brookite is the TiO2 mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1825. That year is not an IMA approval identifier. It is distinct from the rutile and anatase mineral species, from elemental titanium and from unspecified manufactured TiO2 particles. Liu and colleagues studied natural brookite from Magnet Cove, Arkansas, USA, obtained as specimen 8115 from the University of California, Berkeley Earth and Planetary Science collection. Selected black crystals were cleaned with 1 mol/L nitric acid, washed, dried, crushed and ground. Ambient powder XRD and Rietveld fitting support the brookite phase assignment; the subsequent high-pressure experiment is not a microbial assay. Two EDS locations on one ground particle yielded mean reported abundances of O 38.64, Ti 59.23 and Nb 2.13 weight percent. These are localized analyses, not a bulk ore grade, a representative mine inventory or evidence of a chemically pure endmember. Figure S2 compares powder before and after pressing near 8 MPa and supports no apparent phase change during that preparation step. Later compression in a diamond-anvil cell produces pressure- and medium-dependent TiO2 phase mixtures; the source explicitly treats the phase-content diagrams as kinetic, non-equilibrium observations. Its baddeleyite terminology refers to a TiO2 structural polymorph, not formation of the zirconium mineral species ZrO2. No microbial mechanism, titanium extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is asserted by this identity and natural-specimen record.

A natural anhydrous carbonate mineral with the IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula (Na,Ca)3(Sr,Ba,Ce)3(CO3)5. It is grandfathered; the listed 1953 value is an original-description year, not an IMA approval accession. This record denotes the mineral species, not the entire burbankite group, its constituent elements, or a carbonatite ore. Pecora and Kerr (1953) characterized natural hexagonal burbankite from calcite-rich veins at the Vermiculite Prospects, Big Sandy Creek, Bearpaw Mountains, Montana. Powder and single-crystal diffraction support the mineral characterization. Their chemical preparation remained about 96 percent burbankite by grain count, with about 3 percent ancylite and 1 percent other minerals; Table 2 separately gives the impure analysis and an impurity-adjusted calculation. The corrected chemistry is not a direct pure-phase measurement. The authors reported vigorous effervescence in cold dilute (1:5) HCl, but did not establish a leaching yield, rate or isolated rare-earth product. Observed weathering assemblages contained several minerals and do not resolve a unique reaction pathway. A later synthetic Na-Ca-La carbonate with burbankite structure is treated below as an experimental analogue, not as the measured composition of these natural specimens. No dated criticality designation or microbial mechanism is asserted.

Cadmoindite

Cadmoindite is the cadmium-indium sulfide mineral species CdIn2S4, approved as IMA 2003-042 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Chaplygin and colleagues (2004) described natural octahedral crystals from fumarolic crusts at Kudriavy volcano on Iturup Island in the Kuril Islands. Microscopy, fifteen electron-microprobe analyses and powder X-ray diffraction support a cubic thiospinel assignment, compared separately with synthetic CdIn2S4 and the iron analogue indite. The analyzed natural grains contain Fe and Zn and smaller Ge and Se contributions; ideal end-member stoichiometry is not a claim of specimen purity. Crystals occur in both pyrite-associated and pyrite-free assemblages, with cadmium-bearing wurtzite and other phases. The paper reports sampling roughly 15-30 centimetres below the crust surface at outgoing-gas temperatures of 450-600 degrees Celsius. Those are field sampling conditions, not directly observed crystallization temperatures or biological incubation conditions. Formation from cooling gas, including the proposed breakdown of metal chlorides, is inferred from the occurrence and cited gas modelling; it was not demonstrated by a controlled transformation experiment on this mineral. Separate laboratory synthesis conditions and electronic uses of synthetic CdIn2S4 do not establish recovery or deployment of natural cadmoindite. This species is distinct from elemental cadmium or indium, indite, bulk fumarolic crust and manufactured CdIn2S4 considered only by formula. The specimen study does not establish a bulk resource grade or extraction yield. No microbial mechanism or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

Calcioancylite-(La)

A natural lanthanum-calcium carbonate mineral, IMA2021-090, with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula (LaCa)(CO3)2(OH)(H2O). The 2024 ancylite nomenclature distinguishes Ca-dominant calcioancylites from Sr-dominant ancylites, with the suffix denoting the dominant rare-earth constituent. Wang et al. (2023) described the mineral from nepheline syenite in the Gejiu alkaline complex, Yunnan, China; type material is deposited as M16129 in the Geological Museum of China. Individual crystals were 5–20 micrometres. Five electron-microprobe analyses gave mean La2O3 of 24.59 wt% and Ce2O3 of 23.32 wt% (Table 1); this is mixed-REE natural material, not a pure-La endmember. CO2 and water contents were calculated from stoichiometry and charge balance. Raman OH-region bands support a hydrous mineral but do not independently measure its water content. The reported Al2O3 was excluded from the formula as possible microscopic inclusions or surface films, rather than an identified separate phase. A roughly 16 × 7 × 5 micrometre crystal extracted from a polished section was studied by single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 296.15 K. The Pmcn refinement has R1 = 0.0652 for 347 reflections with I > 2 sigma(I). The shared-site La/Ca scattering model, with occupancies 0.66(4)/0.34(4), is distinct from the measured multi-element composition. The official CIF includes no hydrogen positions; its checkCIF report states that structure factors were not supplied and retains formula/model alerts. Table 1's fluorine mean of 0.31 wt% exceeds its printed range of 0–0.16 wt%, and Table 3's formula weight of 726.26 differs from the deposited CIF value of 363.13. These source discrepancies are unresolved; neither value set is silently corrected or treated as an independent composition measurement. The inferred association with late carbonation follows geological textures, not a controlled formation experiment. No microbial mechanism, quantified extraction or product recovery, industrial deployment or inherited criticality designation is asserted.

Calcioburbankite

A natural REE-bearing carbonate mineral, distinct from burbankite and the burbankite group. The September 2026 IMA list gives Na3(Ca,Ce,Sr,La)3(CO3)5 and approval 1993-001. The 1995 original description concerns a Mont Saint-Hilaire holotype, Canadian Museum of Nature catalogue 50804; its precise quarry and geological setting were uncertain. Its surface was partly altered, and a separately encountered La-rich specimen was not pooled with the holotype. Three analyses on three grains support Ca-dominant chemistry. Carbon was detected separately, but the CO2 amount was calculated stoichiometrically, not independently measured. Infrared analysis did not detect OH or water. Powder and precession diffraction established hexagonal symmetry but left three possible space groups; the 1995 paper did not resolve an atomic structure. It cautions that diffraction alone is insufficient to distinguish related species. Table 2 contains inconsistent mean/range entries, including Pr2O3, and a Ca atomic-proportion range apparently duplicated from Na; no disputed range is adopted. Rapid dissolution in 10 percent HCl was a qualitative identification observation without reported time, temperature, loading, yield or isolated product. It is not curated as a recovery mechanism. The later 2001 structure study and a 2024 experimental formation lead remain outside this record's accepted evidence. No criticality designation, microbial activity or industrial deployment is asserted.

Calcioveatchite

Calcioveatchite is the approved calcium-strontium borate species with ideal formula SrCaB11O16(OH)5·H2O and IMA identifier 2020-011 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. It is distinct from the Sr-dominant species veatchite, elemental boron or strontium, and the broad borates commodity. Pekov et al. (2024) characterized natural type material from borehole 130 at 911 m depth in the Nepskoe potassium salt deposit, Siberia, Russia; the Fersman Mineralogical Museum holotype is 97013. The crystals were separated from a water-insoluble residue of the host salt rock. This sample preparation is not a quantified boron extraction or recovery experiment. Electron microprobe analysis of the holotype, averaged over four spots, gave 7.05 wt% CaO, 20.70 wt% SrO and 61.96 wt% B2O3 (Table 1, column 1). Its 10.22 wt% H2O was calculated from the structure because the small crystal could not be analyzed directly for water. A separate gross multi-crystal sample gave 10.07 wt% H2O by the Penfield method, averaging three analyses; these are not two measurements of the same preparation. The holotype empirical formula based on the calculated water is Sr1.23Ca0.78B10.99O16(OH)5·H2O, rather than an experimentally pure ideal end member. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 293(2) K supports monoclinic P21, Z = 2, with the eleven-coordinate cation site Sr dominant [Sr0.902(8)Ca0.098] and the ten-coordinate site Ca dominant [Ca0.686(7)Sr0.314]. Hydrogen positions were located in difference Fourier maps and refined with distance restraints. The site ordering distinguishes this species from veatchite; the paper's formal compositional boundary is Sr1.5Ca0.5B11O16(OH)5·H2O. Its new calcioveatchite observations are from Nepskoe. The inferred possibility of calcioveatchite zones in older Canadian material does not establish the modern identity of every previously studied veatchite specimen. The prose SrO range down to 17.1 wt% appears to include the ideal calculated Table 1 column 2 value of 17.11 wt%; that number is not adopted here as a measured endpoint. Tables 3-7 and Figures 7-8 support the reported structure, but an original CIF/reflection dataset was not acquired and the refinement was not independently repeated. Natural characterization and occurrence do not establish microbial activity, industrial boron recovery or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Carnotite

Carnotite is the potassium uranyl vanadate mineral K2(UO2)2(VO4)2·3H2O. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list recognizes it with grandfathered status G; 1899 is the original-description year, not an IMA approval accession. This mineral-species owner is distinct from the broader carnotite group, elemental uranium or vanadium, mixed uranium ore and dissolved uranyl or vanadate salts. Glasauer et al. (2022) identified K-carnotite together with metatyuyamunite by X-ray diffraction in the final fine fraction of a natural uranium-vanadium sandstone incubated with living Shewanella putrefaciens CN32. The starting assemblage was identified as metatyuyamunite and fritzscheite, rather than a pure carnotite feed. Figure 1b and sections 3.1 and 3.3 support this bounded phase-occurrence comparison. Increased K and decreased Ca in the final fine fraction are consistent with interlayer-cation exchange. The study does not isolate a uniquely biological cause of carnotite formation: the authors recognize both biotic and abiotic pathways, and do not provide a matched final abiotic diffraction series. Section 3.2 describes tyuyamunite-to-carnotite conversion whereas the conclusion names fritzscheite as the precursor; this record assigns neither unique precursor. The shared laboratory experiment used 1.6 g of mixed sandstone in 80 mL defined medium with 10 mM sodium lactate and 1 mM phosphate, nitrogen degassing and autoclaving before inoculation, followed by an anoxic glovebox incubation extending to ten months. Treatments were in triplicate. These three mineral records refer to the same experiment, not independent replications. Bacteria-free solution controls were included, but do not isolate each phase's fate. The mixed-ore spectra support partial V reduction while U remained predominantly U(VI); results from the separate soluble-salt arm must not be transferred to this mineral. Dissolved U was low, rather than established to be exactly zero. Section 3.2 gives a V plateau time of 120 days while Figure 2 labels the time axes in hours, so no exact kinetic endpoint is adopted. The species identity and culture-associated phase occurrence are curated here without a mineral-specific mechanism assertion. Carnotite formation is not established as obligatory, exclusively biological, a pure recovered product or an industrial process. No criticality designation is inherited from its constituent elements.

Catapleiite

Catapleiite is the sodium-zirconium silicate mineral species with ideal formula Na2Zr(Si3O9)(H2O)2. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list records grandfathered status and the year 1850, not a numbered approval accession. It is distinct from calciocatapleiite, elpidite, elemental zirconium and mixed zirconium-bearing rocks. An ideal species formula does not establish the composition or symmetry of every natural grain. Cegiełka and colleagues (2022) assigned catapleiite from microscopy and electron-microprobe data in a loose Dyrnaes River block that they attributed to the Ilímaussaq Green Granite, south Greenland. Figure 3B, Figure 6 and Table 5 document their catapleiite assignment in zircon-bearing aggregates associated with elpidite. This is the same heterogeneous block already described in the elpidite record, not independent sampling or a pure catapleiite feed. The paper does not provide sample-specific diffraction confirmation. Its proposed late-magmatic formation and subsequent hydrothermal sodium loss are geological interpretations, not controlled transformation assays. The detailed analytical appendix and Supplementary Table 1 remain unavailable. Figure 3C labels material SZR while its caption calls it catapleiite; Table 4 and Table 6 repeat IL-356 under different material headings. Main-text and Table 5 sodium ranges also disagree. These unresolved source differences are retained without importing whole-dataset composition ranges or calculating alteration yields. Zubkova and colleagues (2020) distinguish natural catapleiite from the zirconosilicate produced by annealing it at 1000 degrees C. Their silver-exchange experiment used that thermally transformed derivative, whose framework differs from hydrated catapleiite. Its silver-bearing product is not a demonstrated exchange product of the unheated mineral. Figure 1 reuses earlier structural models for the starting mineral and thermal derivative; the new structure determination concerns the silver-exchanged derivative. This study supplies material-boundary context, not a catapleiite recovery yield. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

Its status A and 1988 s.p. entry indicate approval by a special procedure, not a numbered 1988 proposal identifier. The Handbook describes a tetragonal member of the meta-autunite group. This species is distinct from calcium autunite, meta-autunite, dissolved uranium and phosphate-rock feedstock. The study below identifies a laboratory precipitate by comparison with a chernikovite powder pattern; it does not examine a natural chernikovite ore or establish a phase-pure product. No uranium criticality designation is inherited by the mineral.

Childrenite

Childrenite is the Fe2+-dominant aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula Fe2+Al(PO4)(OH)2(H2O), distinct from the Mn2+-dominant endmember eosphorite and oxidized related phases. The September 2026 IMA list records grandfathered status and original-description year 1823. Toupal et al. (2024) characterized two natural grains in granite collected on 11 July 2020 from two outcrops near the southern boundary of the Homolka granite, Czech Republic. Twenty electron-microprobe spots across those two grains gave Fe/(Fe+Mn) from 0.51 to 0.86; these are analytical spots, not twenty independent specimens. Single-crystal diffraction and Raman measurements on Grain A support an orthorhombic Cmca childrenite structure with divalent-cation bond valence at the mixed Fe site. This is specimen-specific structural evidence, not a direct oxidation-state assay of every natural childrenite. It improves on the older Handbook's Bba2 assignment and possible monoclinic interpretation without treating all historical specimens as identical. The crystals show patchy Fe/Mn zoning and probable uraninite inclusions; the inclusions are not independently confirmed as a uranium mineral here. Calculated water raises all microprobe totals above 100 wt%, which the authors attribute to beam-induced partial dehydration; this is not a controlled dehydration experiment. The chemical and structural observations distinguish the investigated grains from a merely compositionally similar ferric phase. The official CIF and main Table 2 disagree on temperature, 273(2) versus 293(2) K, and measured-reflection count, 5429 versus 5682; neither disputed value is adopted as a resolved condition. The CIF's Fe/Ca scattering-site model and formula-sum field are not treated as the measured Fe/Mn/Ca chemistry, and its analytical Si0.04 differs from the main formula's approximately Si0.01. These source limits do not remove the agreement on the unit cell, Cmca symmetry and the 602 observed reflections underlying R1=0.0295. This record establishes natural-mineral identity only, without an experimentally demonstrated formation, extraction, microbial transformation or recovery mechanism. No criticality designation is inherited from constituent elements.

Chlorapatite is the chlorine-dominant apatite mineral species Ca5(PO4)3Cl, distinct from hydroxylapatite, fluorapatite, pyromorphite, generic apatite and mixed phosphate-rock resources. The September 2026 IMA list marks it renamed with 2010 s.p.; this special-procedure notation is not a new-mineral accession. Its findings are not inherited from the pyromorphite dissolution arm or from elemental phosphorus criticality.

Chromite beneficiation tailings

Mixed residual mineral solids from physical beneficiation of chromite-bearing ore. The curated 2018 case is fresh superficial tailings collected in May 2017 at a beneficiation plant in Sukinda valley, Odisha, India, with a separate stockpiled-tailings core used for chemical extraction comparisons. The source describes comminution, desliming and gravity concentration, rather than chromate manufacture. These solids are distinct from the chromite mineral species, unprocessed ore, lateritic overburden, the plant's chromite concentrate and chemically processed chromite ore residues. Reported XRD phases include chromite, goethite, hematite, gibbsite and chlorite; Cr also occurs in nonchromite phases. Table 1 reports 56.7 wt% Fe2O3 and 18.1 wt% Cr2O3 on an XRF oxide-equivalent basis, not quantitative mineral fractions. A separate 2025 fungal study uses two Eti Krom enrichment-tailings feeds labelled olivine and serpentine; both are mixed mineral materials, distinct from the Odisha samples and from pure olivine or serpentine minerals. Neither constituent criticality nor industrial microbial processing is inferred from these feeds' compositions or industrial origins.

Chromite ore processing residue

Chromium-bearing waste from chemical processing of chromite ore, distinct from the chromite mineral species and physical-beneficiation tailings. The curated case is a cementitious, high-lime-process residue from a Glasgow waste-fill site that received material from the Rutherglen Chromite Processing Works. High-lime processing oxidized ore Cr(III) to soluble Cr(VI), followed by aqueous extraction. The 2015 study sampled field-moist material from an exploratory borehole during the M74 motorway project and initially identified it tentatively as COPR from its pale granular appearance and high-pH yellow leachate. Subsequent XRF and XRD characterized a mixed residue rather than proving a pure feed. XRD identified cementitious and hydrated phases, including calcite, portlandite, brownmillerite, pyroaurite, hydrogarnet and brucite; remnant chromite was not detected by that assay. Table 4 reports 3.8 wt% Cr in the XRF composition, without loss-on-ignition correction; this is neither a mineral fraction nor a field-wet feed concentration. This record does not confer a constituent element's criticality designation on the residue or assert commercial microbial processing.

Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts

Naturally occurring layered iron-manganese oxide and oxyhydroxide deposits on exposed marine rock surfaces, commonly seamounts. This resource identity covers the cobalt-bearing, predominantly hydrogenetic crusts formed by accumulation from seawater; it does not denote every hydrothermal encrustation. The heterogeneous crust material is distinct from sediment-hosted polymetallic nodules, constituent cobalt or manganese elements, a pure mineral species, and a processing residue. Maciąg et al. characterize crusts and their altered basalt interfaces from Dirck Hartog Ridge; their sample-specific mineral mixtures are not a universal formula or grade. Collection and physical preparation do not make this geological resource secondary. The laboratory mechanism below records conditional redistribution of cobalt and nickel in whole-crust microcosms; it does not establish a specific receiving phase, a purified metal product or industrial deployment. The resource inherits no constituent criticality.

Coffinite

Coffinite is the uranium-bearing silicate mineral listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as U(SiO4)·nH2O, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1956. That year is not a numbered mineral approval. Coffinite is distinct from uraninite, dissolved uranium, uranium-bearing ores and synthetic mixtures that merely contain uranium and silicon. The variable water term is not a measured hydration number for every specimen. Suzuki et al. (2016) identified natural coffinite nanoparticles in the L3 calcium-carbonate layer of a fracture-filling vein from borehole 07MI07 at the Mizunami Underground Laboratory, Japan. Elemental mapping, selected-area electron diffraction and lattice imaging support their assignment; the particles occur with aluminosilicate and contain other elements including phosphorus, zirconium and yttrium. The authors' proposed microbial origin is an interpretation of a natural setting, not a controlled organism-specific formation experiment. The separate laboratory mechanism below concerns newly formed coffinite on a prepared UO2 pellet, not bioleaching of that natural vein or testing of irradiated spent fuel. No criticality designation is inherited from elemental uranium, and no isolated-metal yield or industrial operation is asserted.

Coking coal

Coal suitable for making coke, treated as an end-use commodity rather than a mineral species, the carbon element, coke itself or all coal. The EIA glossary defines coking coal as suitable bituminous coal. Its separate metallurgical-coal definition includes both coking coal and pulverized coal consumed in steelmaking, whereas the USGS 2026 fact sheet uses coking and metallurgical coal interchangeably in its coke-production scope. This record follows the narrower coke-making identity and records the original EU 2024 coking-coal designation without silently equating all metallurgical-coal uses. The experiment concerns beneficiation of selected Tabas feeds described by the authors as suitable for coking; retained coke-making performance after treatment was not demonstrated.

Coquimbite

Coquimbite is a trigonal aluminium-ferric-iron sulfate mineral, ideally AlFe(III)3(SO4)6(H2O)12·6H2O. IMA-CNMNC proposal 19-F, approved in October 2019, redefined the species to recognize essential aluminium; the September 2026 mineral list retains that formula and redefined status. The older Al-free formula Fe2(SO4)3·9H2O is not the current species definition. Coquimbite and paracoquimbite have related structures and form the coquimbite group; aluminocoquimbite has a different topology and is not a member of that group. In Mauro et al. 2020, a natural Monte Arsiccio specimen was characterized by electron microprobe, spectroscopy and single-crystal diffraction. Twenty microprobe spots gave the empirical formula Al0.96Fe3.11S5.97O24·18H2O, with water calculated from the structure rather than directly measured. Table 3 and the associated CIF model an Al-dominant site with occupancy Al0.946(7)Fe0.054(7). These sample-specific chemical and structural results support the revised identity without implying an exactly ideal bulk composition. The study establishes mineral identity and structure; it does not test microbial formation, extraction or recovery.

Cordylite-(Ce)

A natural barium-rare-earth fluorocarbonate mineral with the IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula (Na,Ca,□)BaCe2(CO3)4(F,O), where □ denotes a vacancy. The authority lists renamed status and 1987 special procedure; this is not an IMA approval accession. This record denotes the Ce species, distinct from cordylite-(La), a rare-earth commodity or a mixed ore. Giester et al. (1998) investigated six specimens by chemical analysis and single-crystal X-ray diffraction and a seventh by X-ray methods alone, from Narssarssuk in Greenland, Mont Saint-Hilaire in Canada, Bayan Obo in China and the Kola Peninsula in Russia. The seventh crystal, original Flink material M.M. no. 392 (Narssarssuk 1*), suffered beam damage that prevented standard microprobe analysis; its qualitative EDX signal establishes Na presence without a quantitative Na concentration. The seven structures were refined in P63/mmc. Attempts in the lower-symmetry alternative P-62c did not give conclusive grounds to prefer it. The paper's idealized formula (Na1-xCax/2)BaCe2(CO3)4F, with 0 <= x <= 1, uses Ce as a proxy for the sum of rare-earth elements, not a measured pure-Ce endmember. X-ray scattering alone cannot resolve the Na/Ca proportion; the separate chemical analyses constrain it. CO2 in Table 5 is calculated by difference, selected Na determinations used direct-current argon-plasma spectrometry, and reliable water analysis was unavailable. These distinctions preclude treating all reported contents as direct microprobe measurements. Comparative and type material support the authors' identification of historical baiyuneboite-(Ce) as cordylite-(Ce) and revision of the older formula; the broader current IMA formula is retained separately from their 1998 model. Printed atomic coordinates and distances were inspected, but deposited anisotropic displacement Table 3 (AM-98-005) was not acquired. No controlled extraction, microbial mechanism, recovery yield, industrial deployment or transferred criticality designation is asserted.

Corkite

Corkite is the lead ferric sulfate-phosphate hydroxide mineral with ideal formula PbFe3(SO4)(PO4)(OH)6, distinct from arsenate-bearing beudantite, plumbojarosite, pyromorphite and elemental lead. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987. Ferrenti et al. (2023) synthesized corkite-bearing powders and characterized their structure and thermal behavior. The best products remained mixed with approximately 9.5 weight percent Pb5(PO4)3Cl; refined phase fractions are not synthesis yield or absolute purity. The authors favor centrosymmetric R-3m from combined diffraction and vibrational evidence, whereas the Handbook lists R3m for natural material. Both diffraction models fit similarly, and substitution, disorder and sample differences remain relevant. The accepted processes are laboratory abiotic synthesis and thermal alteration, without microbial activity, recovered-metal product or industrial demonstration. Criticality is not inherited from constituent elements.

Cuprosklodowskite

Cuprosklodowskite is the copper uranyl silicate hydrate mineral Cu(UO2)2(SiO3OH)2(H2O)4·2H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, equivalent in bulk composition to Cu[(UO2)(SiO3OH)]2·6H2O. Its triclinic P-1 structure is distinct from magnesium-bearing sklodowskite, and the mineral is not elemental copper or uranium. Status G denotes a grandfathered species; 1933 is the original-description year, not a numbered approval accession. Plášil's 2018 study provides original natural-crystal diffraction and hydrogen-position refinement despite the article's Review label. The diffraction crystal came from the National Museum in Prague collection; the article does not establish that it is the Musunoi specimen photographed separately in Figure 2d. Section 3.1 and Figure 4a describe copper's distorted sixfold coordination and the two longer bonds to uranyl oxygen, differing from magnesium's linkage to silicate oxygen in sklodowskite. The original supplementary CIF and Table 2 agree on the unit-cell parameters and R1 = 3.75% for 1033 reflections above I > 3 sigma(I). The CIF retains incomplete publication-template fields and different temperature entries (cell measurement 295(11) K; diffraction ambient 287 K), so a single exact experimental temperature is not imposed here. This record establishes mineral identity and specimen-specific structure; it does not assert a dissolution, microbial extraction, recovery, criticality or industrial-deployment claim.

Donnayite-(Y)

A sodium-strontium-calcium-yttrium carbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula NaSr3CaY(CO3)6(H2O)3. This mineral species is distinct from alicewilsonite-(YCe), a rare-earth element and a mixed ore. The authority lists renamed status and 1987 s.p.; that special-procedure year is not used here as a unique approval identifier. Lykova et al. (2023, Part 1) reexamined seven museum specimens catalogued as donnayite-(Y) cotypes from Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada. Six were reassigned to alicewilsonite-(YCe); CMNMC 39396 was retained as donnayite-(Y) and designated its holotype under approved proposal 22-F. Historical data combined the two species and are not treated as a uniform donnayite dataset. Wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses of the holotype used 20 kV, 10 nA and a 30 micrometre beam with corrections for beam instability. Table 2 reports mean Y2O3 of 10.18 wt% across 17 analyses; H2O and CO2 were calculated from stoichiometry, not directly measured. These specimen assays are not extraction yields. The holotype's single-crystal refinement gave R1 = 0.139 and no satisfactory structural model. The reported triclinic P1 structure with R1 = 0.055 instead used the separate specimen CMNMC 90405 at 293 K. Its model has split carbonate and water positions, unlocated hydrogen, and Dy scattering proxies for lanthanides; it does not directly measure ideal stoichiometry. Published Table 5 gives Rint = 0.092 while the official CIF gives 0.0342 for the equivalent-reflection agreement field; that difference remains unresolved. The official CIF, powder pattern and supplementary bond-valence table were inspected without independent diffraction refinement. The curated evidence establishes natural identity and characterization, not a controlled microbial, extraction or recovery experiment. No criticality designation is transferred from contained elements.

Dzhalindite

Dzhalindite is the indium hydroxide mineral species In(OH)3, listed as approved in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list with the special-procedure year 1967. It is distinct from elemental indium, indite (FeIn2S4), mixed ores and synthetic indium hydroxide products considered only by formula. Kiseleva and colleagues (2008) report a natural occurrence in one quartz-sulfide vein section from 50 metres below the surface at the Bugdaya deposit, eastern Transbaikalia, Russia. They describe 30-94 micrometre crystals in late quartz and zoned In-bearing grains examined by optical microscopy, backscattered-electron imaging and energy-dispersive elemental analysis. Their dzhalindite assignment rests on composition, optical properties and apparent crystal symmetry; X-ray diffraction was unsuccessful because the segregations were too small. Observed Fe zoning does not establish iron speciation or prove substitution within the mineral lattice. The suggested hypogene origin and precipitation from fluids that corroded sphalerite are interpretations, not demonstrated reaction pathways. Temperatures inferred from other phases or analogous veins are not direct measurements on these crystals. This particular occurrence does not establish a universal origin, a bulk resource grade, or an extraction yield. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is assigned.

Elpidite

Elpidite is the sodium-zirconium silicate mineral species with ideal formula Na2ZrSi6O15(H2O)3. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list records grandfathered status and the year 1894; this is not a numbered approval accession. The species is distinct from elemental zirconium, zircon, catapleiite and mixed zirconium-bearing rocks. Cegiełka and colleagues (2022) assigned natural elpidite in a loose block collected from the Dyrnaes River, south Greenland, whose green colour and mineralogy they attributed to the Ilímaussaq Green Granite. Their electron-microprobe analyses, microscopy and zirconium map show elpidite-labelled material enclosing zircon and catapleiite. This is the authors' mineral assignment from a heterogeneous natural specimen, not a sample-specific diffraction confirmation or a pure elpidite feed. Main-paper Table 6 includes both elpidite and altered elpidite; its ideal formula does not imply uniformly stoichiometric analyzed grains. The proposed late-magmatic formation sequence and later hydrothermal sodium loss are interpretations of textures and compositions, not controlled reaction experiments. The cited supplementary analyses and detailed analytical appendix were not acquired, so this record retains bounded main-paper occurrence context without importing whole-dataset ranges or calculating alteration yields. Table 4 and Table 6 both list analysis IL-356 under different material headings; that unresolved assignment is not treated as independent phase proof. No microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

Eosphorite

Eosphorite is the Mn2+-dominant aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula Mn2+Al(PO4)(OH)2(H2O), distinct from Fe2+-dominant childrenite. The September 2026 IMA list records grandfathered status and original-description year 1878. Gatta et al. (2013) examined fragments of one natural crystal from the Chamachhu granitic pegmatite area in Pakistan. Their 22 electron-microprobe spots characterize this crystal rather than 22 independent specimens. The analysis gives Mn0.940 and Fe0.061 atoms per formula unit on a one-P basis; water was calculated using assumed anion stoichiometry. Neutron diffraction at 20 K supports an orthorhombic Cmca model and locates hydrogen sites. The refined mixed metal site contains Fe0.056(1), close to the chemical analysis, without evidence of additional Mn/Fe ordering in this low-Fe specimen. The model assigns O3 to hydroxyl and O4 to statistically shared hydroxyl/water configurations, with the two mirror-related H2 positions mutually exclusive and approximately half occupied. This corrects the hydroxyl/water assignment in Hoyos et al. (1993), whose different natural Taquaral specimen nevertheless supported the same general Cmca framework. The older paper's two-water formula in its introduction and Table 2 is not adopted over the one-water IMA formula and 2013 analysis. The 2013 chemical analysis includes fluorine, but attempted O/F occupancy refinement was not meaningful; its deposited model omits F and must not be read as complete measured composition. Table 5 and the discussion label an O4-H1-O4 angle where the accompanying short contact is described through H2, so no exact value for that disputed hydrogen-bond label is curated. These are specimen-specific structural observations, without a demonstrated extraction, formation or microbial recovery mechanism. No criticality designation is inherited from manganese, aluminium or phosphorus.

Ezcurrite

Ezcurrite is the grandfathered sodium-borate mineral Na2B5O7(OH)3·2H2O in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The list's 1957 entry is the original-description year, not an IMA approval number. Hurlbut and Aristarain's 1967 restudy characterized natural crystals from Tincalayu, Argentina, embedded in borax; possible rivadavite inclusions were invoked to explain the departure of the wet analysis from ideal composition. Cannillo, Dal Negro and Ungaretti's 1973 study established a triclinic P-1 structure containing pentaborate units linked into chains along c, with two tetrahedral and three trigonal boron sites per unit. That study did not repeat the chemical analysis or unit-cell determination for its fragment. Only five of seven hydrogen positions were located; one hydrogen from each water molecule remained unresolved. The 1967 proposed hydroxyl/water partition was superseded by this structural model. The historical comparison with Suhr's synthetic borate does not make nasinite or associated kernite interchangeable with ezcurrite. This mineral species is distinct from elemental boron and the borates commodity; criticality, microbial activity and industrial recovery are not inferred.

Felsőbányaite

Felsőbányaite is the hydrated aluminium hydroxysulfate mineral with ideal formula Al4(SO4)(OH)10·4H2O. The September 2026 IMA list records it as grandfathered, with 1854 in the original-description year column. This owner denotes the mineral species, not elemental aluminium, a bulk mine-water precipitate, or the separately listed hydrobasaluminite. Farkas and Pertlik (1997) characterized natural type-locality felsőbányaite and a Sussex specimen called basaluminite by chemistry and single-crystal diffraction, interpreting the latter as a microcrystalline variety of the former. Their reported monoclinic P21 structure contains aluminium-oxygen layers; beam-induced dehydration reduced structural accuracy, and hydrogen positions were not determined. Later work questions whether poorly ordered materials called basaluminite in acid-mine-drainage studies are structurally equivalent to the crystalline mineral. The 2017 Carrero article's accessible abstract flags this uncertainty; its detailed measurements are not curated here. Nomenclatural synonymy alone therefore does not transfer every basaluminite experiment to this owner. Microbial precipitation, extraction, recovery and industrial deployment are unassessed for this record. No criticality designation is inherited from aluminium.

Tetragonal copper-iron-tin sulfide mineral of the stannite group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula Cu2FeSnS4, renamed status Rn, and approval number IMA 1985-012. Kissin and Owens (1989) characterized the type material from Geological Survey of Canada specimen 14747 (cotypes GSC 65048 polished section A and British Museum (Natural History) BM 1984, 844 grain mount) from a greisen-bordered vein on the 60-m level of the Cligga mine (Cligga Head), Perranzabuloe, Cornwall, United Kingdom, corresponding to the low-temperature polymorph previously referred to in the literature as 'isostannite'. Electron-microprobe analysis of the Cligga mine holotype (Table 1 analysis 4 and Table 4 analysis 1, pp. 675 and 678) yielded Cu 28.9, Fe 8.6, Zn 5.0, Sn 27.0, S 29.5, total 100.9 wt%, corresponding on an 8-atom basis to the empirical formula Cu1.99(Fe0.67Zn0.33)Sigma1.00Sn0.99S4.02, with Fe > Zn at the divalent B site of the kësterite structure. Precession single- crystal and powder X-ray diffraction (Table 6, p. 680) indexed in tetragonal space group I-4 (a = 5.433(36), c = 10.884(89) A, Z = 2), distinguishing ferrokësterite from its high-temperature polymorph stannite (space group I-42m) and from the Zn-dominant end-member kësterite (Cu2ZnSnS4, space group I-4). The 1989 characterization used powder and precession photography without a new single-crystal site-occupancy refinement on the Cligga mine holotype. Distinct from stannite, kësterite, petrukite, sakuraiite, and elemental tin; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Florencite-(La)

Florencite-(La) is the lanthanum-dominant aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula LaAl3(PO4)2(OH)6, distinct from florencite-(Ce), other florencite species, elemental lanthanum and mixed rare-earth ores. The September 2026 IMA list records renamed status and the 1987 special procedure; this is not a numbered species accession or a critical-material designation. Lefebvre and Gasparrini (1980) characterized natural La-rich grains in a Shituru drill-core siltstone, using electron-microprobe chemistry, optical properties and powder diffraction. The Shituru analysis has La as the dominant measured rare earth; Pr was detected qualitatively but not quantified, and water was not measured. Reported rare-earth proportions therefore are not a complete independently measured end-member formula. The diffraction pattern from an extracted 60-micrometre crystal supported florencite identity, while a mixed hematite-florencite concentrate gave only one attributable reflection. The origin was interpreted from geology, with hydrothermal and later supergene alternatives; no controlled formation experiment was performed. Ghignone et al. (2024) separately examined a collection specimen F1 from Igarape Bahia, Brazil. Its unpolished, uncoated SEM-EDS measurements are explicitly semiquantitative, with an oxide total of 35.6 wt%, and cannot be treated as a complete bulk assay or proof of a pure La end-member. The measured Raman spectra of compositionally different florencites are similar; Raman matching alone cannot resolve the dominant rare-earth species. The computed ideal La structure and vibrational modes are models, not a new experimental single-crystal refinement of F1. No microbial mechanism, recovery yield, dated criticality claim or industrial deployment is established by these characterization studies.
