Romanèchite

Romanèchite is a barium-bearing manganese oxide mineral with the IMA formula (Ba,H2O)2(Mn4+,Mn3+)5O10. The September 2026 list marks it approved (A), with "1982 s.p." in the number/year column; special-procedure notation is not a YYYY-NNN accession. The Handbook describes its monoclinic crystal structure. Romanèchite is a mineral species, distinct from barium or manganese elements, cryptomelane, and mixed manganese ores. The historical collective term psilomelane is not treated as an exact synonym for a pure mineral species. No constituent commodity's criticality is inherited. Pracejus's September 1989 thesis supplies mixed-ore experimental context rather than an accepted romanèchite-specific microbial mechanism. Section 5.5 correlates calculated normative mineral proportions of Groote Eylandt cemented pisolites with results from an Enterobacter-species leaching series. Appendix I.3.2 describes 1.89 g heat-sterilized ore, 8 mL 1% w/v molasses, incubation at 32 degrees C, and weekly concentrated H2SO4 addition before centrifugation and supernatant AAS, followed by fresh molasses and bacteria for a 21-week series. The normative romanèchite calculation allocates barium to this phase and neglects its variable potassium, intergrowths and other potential hosts; it is not a direct time-resolved phase abundance measurement. Figures 5.12-5.13 therefore cannot establish a pure-romanèchite bacterial dissolution yield. Matched uninoculated and acid-only results are not presented in the inspected leaching methods, figures or Appendix V.2. The record retains this experimental relevance without assigning a species/strain CURIE, microbial necessity, mineral-specific rate, isolated recovery, or industrial use.

Roquesite

Roquesite is the copper-indium sulfide mineral species CuInS2, listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with renamed status (Rn) and IMA number 1962-001. Picot and Pierrot's original description concerns natural material from Charrier, Allier, France, observed as inclusions in bornite. Powder diffraction, reflected-light microscopy and electron-microprobe observations support its distinction from the associated host minerals. The paper compares this natural material with a separately supplied synthetic CuInS2 specimen; that comparator is not the natural mineral specimen or a microbial product. The synthetic powder pattern contains additional broad central lines whose origin the authors could not test because material was scarce. The natural specimen has reported traces of iron and zinc, so qualitative element-map contrast is not evidence of absolute chemical purity. Both natural and synthetic microprobe analyses total above 100 percent; the authors attribute the excess mainly to sulfur-standard and correction difficulties and also discuss possible reference-metal surface oxidation. Those analyses support the mineral assignment without establishing a closed recovery balance. This record identifies the mineral species, not elemental indium, the entire polymetallic ore or every manufactured material of nominal CuInS2 composition. No microbial mechanism, isolated-metal yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is asserted.

Roscoelite is a vanadium-bearing mica mineral with the ideal formula KV3+2(Si3Al)O10(OH)2 in the September 2026 IMA list. The list records status A and the special-procedure entry 1998 s.p.; that entry is not an original discovery year or a conventional numbered approval. The species is distinct from vanadium as an element, generic vanadium-bearing mica, and mixed shale or ore feeds. Ito's synthetic material was assigned to roscoelite by powder diffraction indexed as a 1M mica; its mixed-valence, nonideal bulk chemistry and microscopic oxide inclusions must not be replaced by the ideal all-V3+ formula. No criticality designation is inherited from vanadium, and neither the natural occurrence nor abiotic synthesis establishes microbial extraction or industrial recovery.

Sakuraiite

Indium-dominant copper-zinc-iron-indium-tin sulfide mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (Cu,Zn,Fe)3(In,Sn)S4 and approval number IMA 1965-017. Originally described by Kato (1965) from the Kanagase vein group of the Ikuno mine, Asago-cho, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan, with a tetragonal or pseudotetragonal subcell (a = 5.455, c = 10.91 A, Z = 2) and an Ag-rich formula (Cu,Zn,Fe,Ag)3(In,Sn)S4, type material from the Ikuno mine (including Kato's 1965 holotype and specimen NSM M-15843 from the Senju-hon vein) was chemically re-examined by Shimizu, Kato, and Shiozawa (1986). Electron-microprobe analyses (Table 1: 5 sakuraiite analyses SK 1-5, 3 coexisting indium-bearing stannite/petrukite analyses ST 1-3, and 2 indium- bearing kësterite analyses KS 1-2, plus step-scan traverses across zoned grains in Figure 3) showed that Kato's 1965 elevated Ag values (3.5-4 wt%) were erroneous (actual Ag 0.10-0.15 wt% in sakuraiite) and established the revised formula (Cu,Zn,Fe)3(In,Sn)S4 with In:Sn atomic ratios reaching 89:11 (analysis SK 2: Cu 1.221, Ag 0.004, Fe 0.436, Zn 1.302, Mn 0.001, Cd 0.032, Sn 0.189, In 0.817, S 3.987 on an 8-atom basis) via coupled (Zn,Fe)In-for-CuSn substitution toward a hypothetical (Zn,Fe)2CuInS4 end-member. Shimizu et al. (1986) did not report new X-ray diffraction measurements, and Kissin and Owens (1989, pp. 684-686) subsequently examined Ikuno mine specimens, identified orthorhombic Pmn21 petrukite and an unindexed Zn > Fe phase, and noted that holotype sakuraiite still required definitive X-ray diffraction characterization to resolve its crystal symmetry and structural relationship to petrukite. Distinct from petrukite, roquesite, stannite, kësterite, and elemental indium or tin; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Saléeite

Saléeite is the magnesium uranyl phosphate decahydrate mineral Mg(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)10 in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1932 denotes its original description, not a numbered IMA approval. It is distinct from lower-hydration metasaléeite, arsenate-bearing nováčekite, aluminium-bearing sabugalite, and elemental magnesium or uranium. Dal Bo and colleagues examined natural saléeite from Shinkolobwe, Democratic Republic of Congo, with associated torbernite. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 293(2) K supports a monoclinic P21/n structure with uranyl-phosphate sheets and hydrated interlayer magnesium. The refined saléeite cell is a = 6.9516(3), b = 19.942(1), c = 6.9667(3) angstrom and beta = 90.586(4) degrees; R1 is 0.0307 for 1990 observed reflections after the reported twin treatment. Qualitative EDS detected U, P, Mg and O but no Fe or As, whereas the crystallographic occupancy model refined 0.97(1) Mg and 0.03(1) Fe at the interlayer cation site. These are different analytical results, not proof of a chemically pure endmember. Hydrogen positions used restrained O-H distances and constrained displacement parameters. This identity and structure evidence does not establish a microbial transformation, an extraction yield, an industrial process or a universal dehydration threshold. No criticality claim is inferred from the mineral's constituents. Deposited reflection data CSD-430599 were not acquired or independently re-refined, and the separate bassetite oxidation discussion is not a saléeite experiment.

Stannite is the mineral species Cu2FeSnS4, recorded as grandfathered (G) with original-description year 1832 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. That year is not an IMA approval identifier. Kiseleva and colleagues (2008, pages 18-21 and Figures 3-4) describe natural Mo-bearing stolzite from the Bugdaya deposit, eastern Transbaikalia, Russia. Sulfoborite

Sulfoborite is a grandfathered magnesium borate-sulfate mineral listed as Mg3[B(OH)4]2(SO4)(OH,F)2 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The list's 1893 entry is a description year, not an approval identifier. Giese and Penna's 1983 single-crystal X-ray study of a natural Westeregeln specimen produced an orthorhombic Pnma structural model with octahedral magnesium, tetrahedral boron and sulfur, hydroxyl groups and a separate fluorine site. Their ideal Mg3[B(OH)4]2(SO4)(OH)F formula and absence of molecular water are conclusions from that structure; they did not chemically analyze the measured crystal. The current species formula's variable OH/F notation is retained rather than replaced with a universally fixed composition. Detailed hydrogen-bond assignments remain qualified by a later neutron study whose complete original was not accessible in this session. This identity record asserts no extraction, transformation or recovery mechanism, industrial deployment or criticality designation. The mineral is distinct from elemental boron, magnesium metal and bulk borate commodities.

Svanbergite

Svanbergite is the strontium aluminium sulfate-phosphate mineral SrAl3(SO4)(PO4)(OH)6, distinct from calcium-dominant woodhouseite, strontium aluminium phosphate goyazite and strontium as an element. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987. Kato and Miura (1977) refined a natural crystal from Dover Andalusite Mine, Nevada, British Museum specimen BM 17702. Single-crystal diffraction used 283 reflections and supported R-3m symmetry, a=6.992(2) and c=16.567(5) angstrom, with R=0.085. This specimen-specific structure contains disordered phosphorus/sulfur tetrahedral sites; the paper does not provide a new chemical analysis of that exact crystal or locate all hydrogen atoms directly. Its separate jarosite specimen and comparisons with earlier structures are not svanbergite synthesis experiments. Stoffregen and Alpers (1987) measured variable natural aluminium phosphate-sulfate grains in three hydrothermal ore deposits. Svanbergite-rich grains accompany alunite or kaolinite in shallower Summitville material, while La Escondida includes intermediate Ca/Sr compositions assigned probable hypogene or supergene origins from textures. Figure 1 shows a grain with subequal Ca and Sr rather than a pure svanbergite endmember; Table 3 and Figure 2 retain compositional variation and calculated water. Replacement or dissolution of apatite in acidic, sulfate-rich alteration is a geological interpretation, not a time-resolved transformation assay or demonstrated microbial mechanism. The 250 degrees C stability diagram in Figure 3 is a calcium-system woodhouseite inference and must not be treated as an experimentally measured svanbergite stability field. The companion woodhouseite record uses the same field-study lineage. Mineral identity and qualified natural alteration context are supported; microbial formation, strontium recovery yield, industrial deployment and mineral-specific criticality are not asserted.

Synchysite-(Ce)

A calcium-cerium fluorcarbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula CaCe(CO3)2F. The authority lists renamed status and identifier 1982-030; these identify this species, not the Nd- or Y-dominant synchysite species, bastnäsite, a rare-earth element or a mixed ore concentrate. Conconi et al. (2025) examined five natural crystals from miarolitic cavities in the Cuasso al Monte granophyre, Italy. Four crystals (FCBN1–FCBN4) supplied monoclinic C2/c average-structure refinements; Raman and SEM–EDS characterization used a subset, and TEM–EDS/electron diffraction used two lamellae from the separate FCBN5 crystal, as specified in Table A1. The crystals show chemical zoning, stacking disorder and inclusions. For FCBN3, Table 3 reports mean Ce contents of 0.44 atoms per formula unit in the core (13 spots) and 0.30 in the outer rim (11 spots), normalized to two cations; these are local composition averages, not recovery measurements or a uniform species formula. Low measured fluorine may reflect beam-induced loss. Fictitious scattering-site occupancies and calculated densities from the diffraction refinements do not directly represent measured chemistry. The proposed screw-dislocation growth sequence and Th-related loss of crystallinity are interpretations of natural microstructure; beam damage and other defects limit causal attribution. No controlled microbial, extraction, or recovery experiment is curated here. Underlying FCF diffraction files were available only upon request and were not acquired; published tables and Appendix A were inspected. No criticality designation is transferred from contained rare-earth elements.

Synthetic graphite

Manufactured crystalline graphite commodity produced industrially by high- temperature graphitization (~3,000 degrees C) of carbonaceous precursors such as calcined petroleum coke and coal-tar pitch. USGS 2021 Minerals Yearbook (Graphite chapter, printed pp. 32.1-32.16) and USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (Graphite (Natural) chapter, printed pp. 92-93) distinguish synthetic graphite from natural flake, amorphous, and vein/lump graphite (cmmmech:natural-graphite and mineral species cmmmech:graphite) and track synthetic graphite across electric-arc-furnace electrodes, unmachined shapes, motor brushes, steelmaking carbon raisers, and lithium-ion battery active anode material (HTS 3801.10, 3801.20, 3801.90, 6903.10, and 8545.11). In the 2023 US Department of Energy Final Critical Materials List (88 FR 51792-51798), DOE evaluated 'Graphite (natural and synthetic)' and 'Graphite--synthetic' in Table 1 (p. 51796, where synthetic graphite alone was scored 'Not Critical' in both short and medium terms) while explicitly noting in Footnote 6 (p. 51796) that the 2022 DOI/USGS Final List of Critical Minerals defined 'graphite' to include both natural and synthetic graphite. This record captures the manufactured synthetic-graphite commodity and its explicit authority scope boundaries without asserting a standalone mineral species identity or microbial mechanism.

Tennantite-(In) is the approved tetrahedrite-group mineral species with ideal formula Cu6(Cu5In)As4S13 and IMA number 2023-011. It is distinct from elemental indium, other members of the tennantite series and the entire polymetallic ore. Voudouris and colleagues describe natural anhedral grains from the Pefka epithermal deposit in Greece, associated with roquesite, galena and tennantite-(Fe) in quartz. Their study reuses the sample investigated by Voudouris and colleagues in 2022, rather than establishing an independent occurrence. Backscattered-electron imaging, wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses and single-crystal X-ray diffraction support the mineral assignment. The seven selected chemical spot analyses near the extracted crystal are part of 86 analyses of the zoned specimen, not seven independent deposits or a bulk ore grade. The refined structural model supports indium at the tetrahedrally coordinated M(1) site; its formal trivalent state is interpreted from chemical and structural constraints rather than measured by a separate valence-sensitive assay. The natural compositions include substitutions and do not equal the ideal end-member formula. Possible intergrowths with lead-bearing phases limit interpretation of minor lead as lattice substitution. The reported powder diffraction pattern and density are calculated; powder diffraction and hardness were not measured on this scarce material. The proposed crystallization sequence and changing fluid conditions are geological interpretations, not controlled reaction experiments. Abstract and Table 3 uncertainties for lead and arsenic differ, so those conflicting uncertainties are not adopted as precise measurements here. No microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is assigned.

The dated US designation concerns the named terbium mineral commodity; it does not assign criticality to every Tb-bearing material. The curated mechanism is a laboratory screening observation using lyophilized cyanobacterial biomass and a synthetic terbium solution, without demonstrated isolated-product recovery.

Tetrahedrite concentrate

A mixed flotation concentrate enriched in source-labelled tetrahedrite, represented by the Strieborná vein feed from the Mária Mine in the Rožňava ore field, eastern Slovakia, studied by Kupka et al. (2025). This extracted geological feed is distinct from a modern tetrahedrite mineral species, elemental copper or antimony, and a waste stream. The source describes tetrahedrite as the principal sulfide, accompanied by siderite and quartz, minor pyrite, arsenopyrite and chalcopyrite, and trace other sulfides. Table 1 reports bulk Cu 25.59, Sb 19.68 and Ag 0.57 wt%. Its approximate phase-proportion prose is inconsistent with its bulk SiO2 value, so no reconciled quantitative mineral assemblage is assigned here. Modern tetrahedrite suffix species are distinct identities; the paper's generic phase label and selected microprobe analyses do not establish a species identity for this heterogeneous feed. No criticality designation is transferred from its constituent elements.

CHEBI:30440
Theisen sludge

Fine-grained flue-dust residue from top-gas scrubbing during copper-shale smelting in a blast furnace, also called Theisenschlamm. The resource scope here is the historical processing waste represented by the Helbra mono-landfill in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. It is distinct from unprocessed copper shale, a mineral species, an elemental commodity and a prepared leaching solution. Meschke et al. (2016) sampled material at a depth of 4 m in May 2015. They measured Cu, Mo, Pb, Sn, Sb and Zn by energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence and Ag, Co, Ge and Re in an aqua-regia extract by ICP-MS. Their Figure 5A identifies zinc and lead as major measured components and reports other measured constituents; the two analytical fractions are not interchangeable measures of complete extractability. This sampled-feed characterization does not establish uniform composition throughout the landfill or a recoverable reserve. The same paper's membrane experiments used prepared Ge/Mo/Re solutions, rather than the sampled sludge or its actual leachate, and its Figure 2 reproduces bioleaching-solution information attributed to Klink et al. (2016). Those distinct evidence streams do not establish a newly verified microbial mechanism, isolated-metal yield or industrial recovery process for this record. No criticality designation is inherited from constituent elements.

Thomasclarkite-(Y)

Hydrated sodium-yttrium bicarbonate-hydroxide mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula NaY(HCO3)(OH)3(H2O)2·2H2O and approval number IMA 1997-047. Grice and Gault (1998) characterized the cotype specimens (CMNMI 81553, CMNMI 81554, and CMNMI 81555, formerly provisional phase UK93) from a large late-stage hydrothermal miarolitic cavity on level 7 of the Poudrette quarry, Mont Saint-Hilaire, Rouville County, Quebec, Canada. Electron-microprobe WDS analysis (2 points on 1 grain, p. 1295) combined with thermogravimetric analysis yielded Na2O 6.72, CaO 0.33, Y2O3 14.52, La2O3 8.63, Ce2O3 17.11, Pr2O3 1.92, Nd2O3 5.63, Sm2O3 1.22, Gd2O3 1.22, Dy2O3 2.04, Er2O3 2.20, Yb2O3 1.32, ThO2 0.54, F 0.17, CO2 12.00, H2O 26.60, O=F -0.07, total 102.10 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 10 anions to the empirical formula (Na0.80Ce0.18Ca0.02)Sigma1.00(Y0.48La0.20Ce0.21Pr0.04Nd0.12Sm0.03Gd0.03Dy0.04Er0.04Yb0.03)Sigma1.22(HCO3)[O6.97F0.03]H9.93. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction refined in monoclinic space group P2 (pseudotetragonal cell a = 4.556(1), b = 13.018(6), c = 4.556(2) A, beta = 90.15(3) degrees, V = 270.2(2) A3, Z = 1, R = 0.055, wR2 = 0.157 for 1616 observed reflections with > 4sigma(F) using reflection twin law (101), twin fraction 0.496(9)) revealed a layered structure with 2-fold orientational disorder of the bicarbonate [HCO3]- groups and half-occupied W7 and OH4 sites. Hydrogen positions were not directly located by X-ray diffraction; the bicarbonate versus carbonate assignment rests on charge balance, C-O bond- valence sums, and infrared absorption bands. Laboratory thermogravimetric analysis showed a two-stage weight loss up to 510 degrees C, and the mineral dissolves readily with strong effervescence in 10% HCl. Distinct from adamsite-(Y), shomiokite-(Y), and elemental yttrium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Tin-copper solder

Tin-copper solder denotes commercially supplied soldering material described as Sn-Cu, rather than elemental tin or copper, a mineral species, or a documented waste stream. Jadhav and colleagues studied material supplied by Taiwan-Solid Enterprises Limited; their methods do not establish a prior service life or recovery from discarded equipment. They report nominal Sn-Cu composition as 63-37%, which is retained as reported rather than corrected to a conventional alloy formulation. Their surface observations suggest a tin-rich coating and a copper-containing interior, so this record does not assert homogeneous bulk alloy composition. Evidence applies to those experimental pieces, not every product sold under the Sn-Cu solder description. No constituent criticality designation is inherited.

Tincalconite

Tincalconite is the Na2B4O5(OH)4(H2O)3 mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1878 rather than a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from borax, kernite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Pabst and Sawyer characterized clear natural crystals from a Searles Lake drill core at about 116 feet depth; direct crystallization from brine was their interpretation of the occurrence, not an observed formation experiment. Giacovazzo et al. refined synthetic crystals grown from aqueous borax near 80 degrees C in trigonal R32. Luck and Wang later refined at 291(2) K a synthetic crystal obtained from layered aqueous sodium borohydride and tetraheptylammonium iodide in acetone, also in R32. Their partially occupied water-oxygen model favored Na6[B4O5(OH)4]3·8H2O, equivalent to 2.667 waters per Na2B4O5(OH)4 unit, rather than the three waters retained in the current IMA formula. Their freely refined O12 occupancy was 0.337(5); this is a crystallographic model result, not a measured water extraction yield or a new accepted mineral species. The 2002 Table 1 formula H28B12Na6O27 omits oxygen relative to the article's stated hydrated formula; its formula mass is therefore not adopted. Natural species identity, synthetic structural models and experimentally transformed mixed material remain separate. No commodity criticality, microbial activity or industrial recovery claim is inherited.

Titanite

Titanite is the calcium titanium silicate mineral with ideal formula CaTiO(SiO4), also written CaTiSiO5. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list records approved status A and the special-procedure token 1967 s.p.; this is not a numbered IMA proposal. Sphene is a historical name used in the processing literature. This species is distinct from elemental titanium, titanium metal, TiO2 polymorphs and titanite-bearing ore or flotation-tail mixtures. A primary laboratory study supports hydrochloric-acid decomposition of a titanite-rich mixed concentrate and formation of a titanium/silica solid, with important feed and analytical limitations. Criticality, microbial activity and industrial recovery performance are not inferred.

Titanium metal

Titanium in metallic commercial forms, considered as a raw-material commodity. USGS distinguishes titanium sponge metal and downstream metal forms from titanium dioxide pigment and mineral concentrates. Sponge is one metal form, not the entire commodity. This record is distinct from the titanium element as a chemical identity, titanium-bearing minerals, titanium oxides and any particular alloy formulation or waste stream. Its pooled results do not establish sponge-specific recovery, microbial enhancement or production of pure titanium metal.

Todorokite

Todorokite is the hydrous manganese oxide species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with formula (Na,Ca,K,Ba,Sr)1-x(Mn,Mg,Al)6O12·3-4H2O (PDF page 218). Its status is approved; the accompanying 1962 s.p. entry identifies action by special procedure, not a modern approval-number CURIE. The Handbook of Mineralogy describes monoclinic material with variable cation composition and hydration in analyzed natural specimens. Its older generalized formula and specimen analyses are not substituted for the current IMA formula. Documented occurrence includes weathering or hydrothermal alteration of manganese-bearing minerals and deep-sea manganese nodules; these contexts do not specify a universal abundance or ore grade. The Handbook's geological term secondary mineral describes formation by alteration, not a material generated by industrial processing. This species is distinct from elemental manganese, a bulk manganese ore or nodule, and a manganese oxalate product. No microbial mechanism or criticality designation is assigned here.

Torbernite

Torbernite is a copper uranyl phosphate mineral with formula Cu(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)4·8H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, which gives status A and the designation 1980 s.p.; this special-procedure designation is not a numbered mineral approval identifier. Locock and Burns grew synthetic torbernite crystals at approximately 5 degrees C over two months by diffusion of phosphate and uranyl nitrate into copper-bearing silica gel, then measured an epoxy-coated crystal by room-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction. They refined a tetragonal P4/nnc structure with twelve water groups per formula unit and uranyl-phosphate sheets. Copper has four short bonds to coordinating water groups and two longer contacts to uranyl oxygen atoms, interpreted as Jahn-Teller-distorted (4+2) coordination. The remaining water groups form square-planar sets above and below the copper plane. The proposed hydrogen-bond network uses difference-map hydrogen positions constrained to O-H bond lengths and fixed displacement parameters. The paper presumes equivalence to natural torbernite from agreement of unit-cell dimensions; it did not analyze a natural torbernite crystal. Its separate metatorbernite, zeunerite and metazeunerite arms have different preparations and structures. In particular, eight-water metatorbernite, its twinning and 88.3(6)% copper occupancy are not torbernite results. Structural comparison with the separately prepared eight-water phase supports a distinction between hydration states but is not a direct time-resolved dehydration experiment or recovery measurement. The article references deposited observed/calculated structure factors that were not acquired in this investigation; no independent diffraction re-refinement is claimed. Torbernite is distinct from metatorbernite, the autunite group, uranyl ions and elemental uranium or copper. This laboratory structural evidence establishes neither microbial extraction nor isolated-product recovery, industrial deployment or criticality inherited from either element.

Triphylite

Triphylite is the lithium iron(II) phosphate mineral LiFe2+(PO4), listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as grandfathered, with original-description year 1834 rather than an approval identifier. It is distinct from Mn2+-dominant lithiophilite and oxidized, lithium-deficient members of the group. Losey2004 characterized natural pegmatite crystals by electron microprobe and single-crystal diffraction in the Pbnm setting of orthorhombic space group 62; Pmnb in the Handbook is another setting. The natural samples are solid solutions, including Mg substitution, not all pure LiFePO4. Lithium was not independently measured in that study: Li2O was assumed for matrix correction and Li-site occupancy fixed during refinement. The accepted transformation study uses a separately characterized natural triphylite specimen with minor sarcopsides visible microscopically, and demonstrates abiotic oxidation with spatially resolved lithium depletion, not microbial weathering or a recovered lithium product. The historical ferrisicklerite product name in the 2013 original is discredited under the 2022-approved nomenclature published in 2023; that publication classifies the studied Tri-77 and Tri-87 products as heterosite. No constituent-element criticality designation is inherited.

Tunellite

Tunellite is the SrB6O9(OH)2(H2O)3 mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with approved status A and special-procedure notation 1967 s.p., not a unique approval identifier. It is distinct from veatchite, elemental boron and strontium, and mixed borate ores. The monoclinic P21/a structure contains hexaborate units with three boron triangles and three tetrahedra, polymerized into sheets. The 1994 refinement of California specimen CMN 57614 located eight hydrogen sites using X-ray difference-Fourier maps with soft O-H distance constraints; seven sites participate in interpreted hydrogen bonds, five between sheets. This superseded the 1964 geometrical proposal, which had not located hydrogen sites. Separate Turkish material supplied the historical heating experiments below. No criticality, microbial mechanism or industrial deployment is inferred.

Tungsten skarn-processing tailings

Residual mineral solids generated by processing tungsten-bearing skarn ore. The curated case is historical tailings in the Smaltjärnen repository at the closed Yxsjöberg tungsten, copper and fluorspar mine in Sweden. The processing plant used gravity separation, magnetic separation and flotation. The characterized layered material contains scheelite among mixed silicate, carbonate, sulfide and other minerals; composition and particle liberation vary by sampled layer. This resource is distinct from tungsten as an element, pure scheelite, unprocessed ore, waste rock and a saleable concentrate. Hällström et al. document scheelite alteration, hydrous ferric oxide associations and tungsten transport in a field investigation of this repository; those geochemical observations do not establish microbial causation. No criticality designation is inherited from constituents, and the laboratory results below do not characterize all tungsten tailings.

Uranopilite

Uranopilite is the uranyl sulfate oxide hydroxide hydrate mineral with the September 2026 IMA formula (UO2)6(SO4)O2(OH)6(H2O)6·8H2O. Its grandfathered status G and original-description year 1882 are not a numbered approval accession. It is distinct from elemental uranium, a uranium commodity, zippeite and phases historically called metauranopilite. Burns determined the triclinic P-1 structure from a natural Joachimsthal, Bohemia specimen in Harvard Museum collection 89612. The structure contains uranyl sulfate chains with six coordinated and eight interstitial water groups per formula unit. Hydrogen positions were not directly located; the hydrogen-bond model and hydroxyl/water assignments used crystal-chemical and bond-valence arguments. The historical (UO2)6(SO4)(OH)10·12H2O formulation has the same total elemental composition but a different partition of hydroxyl and molecular water. The later natural Cervena-vein study confirmed the structure with substantial twinning and refinement limitations. Its Table 15 water content was calculated from the assumed fourteen-water structure, not independently measured. Natural crystals in ore fractures support occurrence in an alteration assemblage; they do not establish a controlled formation rate, exact formation pH or microbial causation. This record accepts natural identity and structural evidence, with thermal transformations deferred. No criticality designation, extraction yield or industrial recovery is inferred.

Veatchite

Veatchite is the strontium borate mineral species with ideal formula Sr2B11O16(OH)5·H2O in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1938. That year is not a sequential approval identifier. Its three named polytypes are veatchite-1A, veatchite-1M and veatchite-2M, historically called veatchite-A, p-veatchite and veatchite, respectively. These are not three separate species owners. Veatchite is distinct from elemental strontium or boron, the borates commodity, and the Ca-Sr-ordered species calcioveatchite, SrCaB11O16(OH)5·H2O. Grice and Pring (2012) determined the structures of separate natural specimens using single-crystal X-ray diffraction: NMNH 145911 from Emet, Turkey, for triclinic 1A with space group P-1; NMNH 113264 from Reyershausen, Germany, for monoclinic 1M with P21; and RG701/1 from Sussex, New Brunswick, for monoclinic 2M with Cc. The last specimen replaced the preserved California type crystal and must not be attributed to that type locality. Borate layers and their stacking distinguish the polytypes; the authors caution that their powder patterns alone do not satisfactorily distinguish them. Hydrogen positions were located by difference Fourier maps and refined, but no new chemical analyses were performed on the two type specimens. The paper's 2M Sr/Ca refinement has a slightly Ca-dominant smaller cation site and is explicitly discussed as potentially a new species; it is not a pure Sr end-member measurement. Pekov et al. (2024) subsequently establish the distinct calcioveatchite species and emphasize site occupancy in the boundary with veatchite. They do not directly reanalyse the 2012 RG701/1 crystal, so its exact modern species assignment remains a specimen-level qualification here. The 2012 temperature/pressure associations are geological interpretations with unknown precise parameters, not controlled polytype-transition experiments. Natural mineral characterization and geological occurrence do not establish microbial activity, boron recovery, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

The accepted study uses violarite broadly for intermediate Fe–Ni thiospinel compositions rather than proving an ideal FeNi2S4 product. Its experiments were abiotic and do not inherit constituent criticality or demonstrate microbial production.

Voltaite

Voltaite is a cubic mixed-valence iron sulfate mineral with the September 2026 IMA ideal formula K2Fe(II)5Fe(III)3Al(SO4)12(H2O)18. This species is distinct from the voltaite mineral group, tetragonal pertlikite and the magnesium-, zinc- or ammonium-dominant analogues. Zhitova et al. (2023) characterized two samples labelled voltaite: Ni4225 from a coal-fire pseudofumarole in Nikitovka and SCCIII-14-20s from the Bolshoi Semiachik geothermal field. Their selected crystals were refined in cubic Fd-3c at 293 K, without clear evidence of lowered symmetry. The surrounding assemblages include other sulfates and are not pure voltaite feeds. Composition was measured by EDS on beam-sensitive hydrated grains; Fe(II)/Fe(III) proportions were calculated by charge balance, water was assigned from stoichiometry, and totals for these unpolished samples were normalized. Table 4 gives approximately one monovalent cation per formula unit for these samples, whereas the ideal formula and fully occupied structural A site imply two; this unresolved analytical/refinement discrepancy is not silently corrected. SCCIII-14-20s is also close to the Fe/Mg species boundary. These observations support a qualified natural-specimen identity record, without transferring every sample composition to ideal voltaite or treating geological occurrence as a controlled formation experiment. No microbial mechanism, extraction, recovery yield, industrial deployment or criticality designation is curated.

Weeksite

Potassium uranyl silicate hydrate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (K)2(UO2)2(Si5O13)(H2O)2·2H2O, status A, and special-procedure approval year 1962 s.p. (not a numbered IMA-XXXX-YYY accession). Outerbridge, Staatz, Meyrowitz, and Pommer (1960) described the holotype from opal-fluorite-calcite veinlets in porphyritic rhyolite at the Autunite No. 8 claim, east side of the Thomas Range, Juab County, Utah, USA, and documented nine additional occurrences in Utah, California, New Mexico, Wyoming, Pennsylvania, Texas, Arizona, and Chihuahua, Mexico. Microchemical analysis of ~100 mg of purified Thomas Range type material (Table 3, p. 46: SiO2 33.6, UO3 51.5, K2O 5.5, BaO 1.4, CaO 1.1, Na2O 0.7, Al2O3 0.6, CO2 0.3, H2O 6.6, Fe2O3 <0.1, sum 101.3 wt%) and single-crystal precession / powder X-ray diffraction led the 1960 authors to propose the orthorhombic Pnnb formula K2(UO2)2(Si2O5)3·4H2O (a = 14.26(2), b = 35.88(10), c = 14.20(2) A, Z = 16). Later structural studies cited in the IMA Master List (including the paywalled second reference Mineralogical Magazine 90 (2026), 653, which was not acquired at curation) revised the silicate-sheet stoichiometry from (Si2O5)3 (6 Si per 2 U) to (Si5O13) (5 Si per 2 U); both the 1960 analytical formula and the current IMA formula are retained with explicit attribution. Outerbridge et al. (1960) also demonstrated laboratory hydrothermal synthesis of weeksite and its Na analogue in sealed Pyrex tubes at 150 degrees C. Distinct from haiweeite, boltwoodite, uranophane, and elemental uranium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Woodhouseite

Woodhouseite is the calcium aluminium sulfate-phosphate mineral CaAl3(SO4)(PO4)(OH)6, distinct from strontium-dominant svanbergite, calcium aluminium phosphate crandallite and calcium as an element. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987. Lemmon (1937) described natural crystals from quartz veins adjoining and penetrating andalusite deposits on White Mountain, Mono County, California. Geometrical crystallography, optical observations and wet chemical analysis of hand-sorted crystals supported the new mineral. Its analysis contains minor substituents and a phosphate-sulfate imbalance; Lemmon explicitly considered a single analysis insufficient to prove the proposed substitution. This historical description is not a modern single-crystal refinement. Stoffregen and Alpers (1987) subsequently measured natural aluminium phosphate-sulfate grains by electron microprobe at Summitville, La Granja and La Escondida. Calcium-rich grains approaching woodhouseite occur at depth in Summitville and at La Granja, where small grains appear to replace apatite and contact pyrophyllite. Variable Ca/Sr and phosphate/sulfate ratios, minor additional cations and calculated rather than measured water distinguish these grains from pure ideal endmembers. Figure 1 depicts an approximately equal Ca/Sr grain, not pure woodhouseite. Apatite dissolution or replacement during advanced argillic alteration is the authors' field-textural interpretation; there was no controlled formation experiment, reaction time series or microbial assay. Their 250 degrees C, 40-bar stability diagram uses assumed aqueous compositions and an inferred woodhouseite boundary because direct thermodynamic data were unavailable to that study. It is not a measured formation threshold, and its hydroxyapatite model omits fluoride/chloride effects. The companion svanbergite record uses the same field study. These sources establish mineral identity and qualified natural alteration context, not microbial formation, elemental extraction yield, isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Xenotime-(Gd)

Xenotime-(Gd) is the gadolinium-dominant xenotime species with ideal formula Gd(PO4), approved as IMA 2023-091. Its tetragonal I41/amd structure distinguishes it from monoclinic monazite-(Gd), despite their shared ideal formula. Ondrejka et al. (2024) characterized natural domains up to 20 micrometres across within xenotime-(Y) from the Zimna Voda quartz vein near Prakovce, Slovakia. Electron microprobe analyses at and near the holotype lamella average 29.16 wt% Gd2O3 across six points in Table 2, with substantial Y and Dy; these are mixed mineral compositions, not pure GdPO4, bulk ore grade or recovered gadolinium yield. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, Fourier-transform patterns and Raman observations support xenotime-type identity. Single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction were not obtained; Table 3 is a calculated powder pattern. The cell parameters from 25 Fourier-transform reflections and those estimated from weighted end-members are separate results. Density and refractive index are calculated, and several physical properties remain unmeasured. The 2026 corrigendum replaces Figure 4 because the black Raman traces for xenotime-(Y) and xenotime-(Gd) were interchanged; its authors retain the original text and interpretations. The proposed hydrothermal origin does not establish a controlled formation mechanism, microbial activity, recovery performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Xenotime-(Yb)

Xenotime-(Yb) is the ytterbium-dominant xenotime mineral with ideal formula Yb(PO4), approved as IMA 1998-049. It is distinct from elemental ytterbium, xenotime-(Y), xenotime-(Gd) and mixed xenotime concentrates. Buck et al. (1999) described microscopic natural grains in ferrian muscovite aggregates from the SHE-5 pegmatite of the Shatford Lake group, southeastern Manitoba, Canada. Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analyses show substantial Y and other rare-earth substitution. The mean of three spots on the diffraction-analyzed grain contains 36.37 wt% Yb2O3 and totals 95.75 wt%; a separate embedded grain contains 32.27 wt% Yb2O3 and totals 98.27 wt%. The authors attribute the low first total mainly to charging in nonconductive epoxy; this explanation was not independently established and the values are not corrected here. These are grain compositions, not ore grades or extraction yields. Powder diffraction of three grains supports a tetragonal xenotime pattern consistent with I41/amd and refined cell dimensions a = 6.866(2) and c = 6.004(3) angstrom. Suitable material for single-crystal structure refinement was unavailable. Powder intensities were estimated visually, without an internal standard or film-shrinkage correction. The reported density of 5.85 g/cm3 was calculated, not measured. Geological discussion of fluoride complexing does not establish a controlled formation, microbial extraction or recovery process. No industrial deployment or jurisdiction-specific criticality designation is asserted.

Yanomamite

Yanomamite is the hydrated indium arsenate mineral species In(AsO4)(H2O)2, approved as IMA 1990-052 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Botelho and colleagues (1994) characterized natural crystals from quartz-topaz greisen at the Mangabeira tin deposit, Goiás, Brazil, using microscopy, electron-microprobe analysis and single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction. The orthorhombic Pbca assignment is supported by natural specimens and a separate synthetic comparator; a matching chemical formula alone does not identify the mineral. Natural crystals contain minor Fe and Al and occur intergrown with or coated by indium-bearing scorodite. Even the three selected single crystals retained minor scorodite, whereas the selected powder material showed no significant scorodite reflections. Water in the reported empirical composition was calculated rather than directly measured because of these impurities. The authors considered both supergene and hydrothermal origins, favoring a hydrothermal association with the main cassiterite stage while explicitly describing the origin discussion as speculative. The actual indium source and transport were not established. These natural alteration associations do not constitute a microbial transformation experiment. This mineral is distinct from elemental indium, scorodite, mixed greisen feed and industrial secondary resources; geological replacement does not make it processing waste. The characterized grains establish neither a bulk resource grade nor extraction performance. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

Yusupovite

Yusupovite is the sodium-zirconium silicate mineral species with ideal formula Na2Zr(Si6O15)(H2O)3, approved as IMA 2014-022. It is a monoclinic C2/m dimorph of orthorhombic elpidite, rather than another name for elpidite or elemental zirconium. Agakhanov and colleagues (2015) characterized natural grains in pegmatitic rock samples collected from the Darai-Pioz glacier moraine in Tajikistan. The grains occur within reedmergnerite-bearing material with quartz and other associated minerals; this is not a pure bulk ore or an in-place deposit survey. Powder and single-crystal diffraction, electron-microprobe analyses, microscopy and infrared spectroscopy support the assignment. The mean of ten point analyses and the refined site populations describe a compositionally substituted specimen containing K, Cs, Y and minor Hf, not an exact realization of the ideal end-member. Its water content was calculated from the structure refinement, yielding about 2.52 H2O per formula unit; it was not an independent direct water measurement. The authors' structural comparison with elpidite does not demonstrate a time-resolved transformation between the minerals. Their discussion of ion exchange and radionuclide containment is prospective and draws on separate, earlier elpidite experiments. No yusupovite exchange capacity, microbial mechanism, metal recovery, industrial deployment or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

Zippeite

Zippeite is the potassium uranyl sulfate hydroxide hydrate mineral with the September 2026 IMA formula K2[(UO2)4(SO4)2O2(OH)2](H2O)4, redefined status Rd and entry 1971-029a. It is a mineral species, distinct from the zippeite group, other cation-dominant group members, elemental uranium and a uranium commodity. The natural species must not be equated without qualification to the K3, three-water synthetic compound called zippeite by Burns and colleagues in 2003. The latter was refined in C2; the natural material discussed by Plasil and colleagues in 2014 was indexed in C2/m. Their original powder-XRD result for fine-grained zippeite II from the Cervena vein, Jachymov, Czech Republic gave a = 8.844(1), b = 14.115(2), c = 8.856(1) angstrom, beta = 104.785(8) degrees and V = 1068.9(3) cubic angstrom (Table 29). This is distinct from the zippeite I single-crystal values reproduced from their earlier 2011 study. Figures 13-14 show crystalline aggregates and powdery coatings in the natural weathering assemblage. The proposed later precipitation of the powdery material is a petrographic interpretation, not a timed or controlled conversion. Formation pH, temperature, aqueous composition and uranium mass balance were not directly established for that event. This record accepts natural identity and occurrence evidence; no criticality designation, microbial process, extraction yield or industrial recovery is inferred.

Zircon

Zircon is the zirconium silicate mineral species Zr(SiO4), listed as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. It is distinct from elemental zirconium, zirconia (ZrO2), zircon-bearing sand or concentrates, and other ZrSiO4 polymorphs. Hazen and Finger (1979) characterized two fragments of one natural, nonmetamict, gem-quality crystal from the Finsch Pipe kimberlite near Kimberley, South Africa, using single-crystal X-ray diffraction under pressure. Their specimen description reports nearly pure zircon with 1.2 weight percent HfO2 and 26 ppm uranium; these are specimen-specific values, not universal mineral composition or a resource grade. The refinements support a tetragonal I41/amd structure with four formula units per unit cell. Measurements extended to 48.1 kbar; higher-pressure phase transitions discussed in that paper are predictions or references to other studies, not transformations observed in this experiment. The two fragments are not independent geological occurrences. This identity and structural evidence does not establish microbial transformation, recovery, industrial deployment or a criticality designation for the mineral.

Zirconolite

Zirconolite is a zirconium-bearing oxide mineral listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with formula (Ca,Y)Zr(Ti,Mg,Al)2O7 and redefined status. Its 1989 special-procedure entry is not a numbered new-mineral approval. CaZrTi2O7 is the simplified composition used in the cited nomenclature and natural-specimen study, not the measured formula of every grain. The IMA-approved nomenclature published by Bayliss et al. (1989) uses the unsuffixed name for metamict or undetermined-polytypoid material and distinguishes the 2M, 3T and 3O layered variants from cubic zirkelite. This record does not assign a particular polytypoid, space group or synthetic ceramic composition to an uncharacterized natural specimen. Bellatreccia et al. (1999) studied a natural polycrystalline aggregate collected at Jacupiranga, São Paulo, Brazil, from the locality historically associated with the name zirkelite. It was explicitly a different specimen from the historical type specimen. One hand-picked grain yielded no diffraction pattern after 48 hours in a Gandolfi camera; the authors assigned zirconolite using the metamict state and chemical composition. Three crystals examined by electron microscopy and electron microprobe showed oscillatory, sector or irregular compositional zoning. Their zirconium-bearing chemistry also included niobium, thorium, uranium, hafnium and rare-earth elements; this is specimen chemistry rather than a bulk resource grade. Table 3 separates new zirconolite analyses from the chemically distinct intergrown calzirtite. Point analyses and images support the natural occurrence, but no structure refinement of the unheated metamict specimen establishes a 2M identity. Historical heat-treated lattice parameters in Table 2 are reused from other studies, not newly measured natural-crystal structures in this investigation. The specimen's reported heavy-mineral sand provenance and carbonatitic chemical affinity do not resolve its original host rock unambiguously. Fine lamellae approach the microprobe spot size, so intermediate analyses can mix adjacent zones.
